You become a part of their lives and you get to watch their children grow. I loved that [aspect] of the job,” she said. articles.text: After yearlong lockdown, This year’s parade theme: Back to the Future This year, Piedmont’s July 4 parade, the city’s most well-attended event for over 50 years, will continue in a non-traditional fashion. Instead of the parade taking place on Highland Avenue, a small group of vehicles with Mayor Teddy Gray King will wind its way through many neighborhoods for an hour. The flotilla will be led by the Barrelhouse Jazz Band on the W.A. Rose flatbed truck. The idea of a small parade moving through town avoids the usual gathering of large numbers of people on Highland Avenue but allows a semblance of a return to normalcy after more than a year of no public events due to the COVID-19 pandemic. articles.text: Bouquets to Art returns to San Francisco’s de Young Museum for its 37th year, with floral exhibits and programs open to the public from June 8 through June 13. For one week, more than 100 floral designers will converge at the de Young to showcase arrangements inspired by the museum’s paintings, sculptures, and architecture. Bouquets to Art is one of the Fine Arts Museum of San Francisco’s most popular and well-attended events every year. The event is presented by the volunteer members of the fine arts museums - and draws nearly 800,000 visitors a year, with net proceeds of more than $7 million. Funds from the event help underwrite special exhibitions, conservation projects, and educational programming. For the first time, Bouquets to Art will include a “virtual visit.” This 360-degree tour provides a closer look at each floral arrangement and design in the galleries. The virtual tour is free for museum members and $10 for the general public. Soho Sakai, longtime exhibitor and presenter, will lead an ikebana Valerie Ow, co-owner at J. Miller Flowers on Piedmont Avenue, designed this bouquet for Bouquets to Art in 2018 inspired by “Flora and Fauna of the Pacific” by Miguel Covarubias.

articles.text: This time last year, we were trying to figure out how we were going to survive a summer of COVID and all of the social restrictions. And then, like a breath of fresh air, the Piedmont Recreation Department came to our rescue. They announced they’d be hosting a modified in-person day camp, Camp (Almost) Everything, starting June 1, 2020. This was literally the first summer camp in the Bay Area that gave children a chance to be together again since schools abruptly closed in March. While school districts around the country continued to debate about the best path forward for kids, PRD quietly and quickly got to work and figured out how to safely meet the social and emotional needs of Piedmont kids. As Erin Rivera recently noted at the City Council meeting, “We were on the cutting edge, keeping kids happy. We followed the science, we followed the safety. We did really amazing things.” On behalf of so many grateful Piedmont parents, I would like to thank Erin and the rest of the Recreation Department team for the many amazing things they accomplished for our families over the last year. The wonderful staff showed up every day for our kids, helping them thrive and feel normal in this very abnormal year. They helped keep our kids healthy from the devastating emotional effects of isolation. Here are a few words of gratitude from local families. were really missing their teachers and coaches. articles.text: A friend of mine who belongs to the Greek Orthodox church reminded me that the faithful of that denomination greet one another in the Easter season with, “Christ is risen” and the other replies, “He is risen indeed!” What a beautiful way to connect our ordinary daily speech with our faith in the basic reality of Christianity. But something else is in play here: the sense of community, in which people are conscious that there is something important they have to share. The Christian scriptures, beginning with the letters of St. Paul and later with the gospel accounts, clearly indicate that the followers of Jesus were acutely aware of belonging together, that togetherness was a hallmark of their existence. It was in gathering together with the common purpose of remembering the Lord’s words and deeds that they would fulfill his command to love one another. That in turn would reveal the substance of the one great commandment to love God and one’s neighbor as oneself. The practical outcome of this is found in the Lord’s declaration: As long as you did it to one of the least of my people, you did it to me. This expansiveness is different from an attitude so prevalent today in which the narrow approach of personal autonomy and social restrictiveness result not only in pain and suffering but in downright injustice. articles.text: The Oakland-Fukuoka Sister City Association (OFSCA) is hosting a culinary fundraiser event via Zoom in honor of its 60th anniversary. The organization is partnering with Daughter Thai Kitchen and Urban Legend Cellars to feature their food and wines in support of local restaurants and wineries, and to raise funds for the association’s upcoming 60th anniversary. OFSCA helps to foster and promote cultural awareness, understanding, and friendship between the people and cities of Oakland and Fukuoka, Japan, and supports a summer exchange program for students in the U.S. and Japan. Ticket holders will pick up a prepared meal and wines to finish at home while watching Chef Kasem Saengsawang demonstrate the food and winemakers Steve and Marilee Schaffer discuss their wine pairings. The meal kit features Mieng Kum Bites and Shrimp Pad Thai, a dish that can be easily prepared within 30 minutes. All elements are prepped and pre-cooked to cut down on cooking time. Chef Saengsawang will demonstrate step-by-step how to cook the meal. For a wine pairing, you may choose either or both a 2019 Vermentino and 2019 Rosato di Barbera. The deadline for tickets is Thursday, June 10. The event itself is Wednesday, June 16, from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m. via zoom. Purchase tickets via Eventbrite at https://www. eventbrite.com/e/ofsca-fundraiser-a-culinary-libation-journey-through-the-east-bay-tickets-154282640531?ut m-medium=discover y&ut m-camp a i g n = s o c i a l & u t m - c o n - tent=attendeeshare&aff=escb&utm-source=cp&utm-term=listing.

articles.text: Being a California resident requires some degree of drought familiarity. Currently three quarters of the state is experiencing extreme drought. Last year at this time, preceding historic wildfires, 39% of the West was experiencing drought, and now that number is up to 83%. Distressingly, 38% of the West is currently experiencing “exceptional” drought, an event that typically occurs one to These grim statistics show that drought has become part of California life, and there is a growing need to deal with the root problems. Effects of drought can range from more intense and fareaching wildfires, to diminished agricultural returns, to increased prices for drinking water. These outcomes are likely to become more common with the advanceWater management practices can affect drought impacts. Since 1979, California’s population has doubled, but water infrastructure projects have lagged behind. The State Water Project, one of the largest public water projects in the world, began in the 1950’s and is still being improved upon today. However, many water projects that residents and farmers still rely on were constructed in the 20th century, and now require Aging infrastructure struggles are compounded by California’s natural precipitation patterns. Partly due to the coastline and inland mountain ranges, California has some of the most variable patterns of rain of any state. Northern California is currently in one of the largest rainfall deficits in modern history. The paltry rainfall can be partly attributed to a La Niña year. Drier conditions are to be expected, but this year is atypical. Humans continue to release greenhouse gases, which can exacerbate naturally occurring weather events such as La In addition to weather patterns and water infrastructure issues, there are often conflicts over the best way to secure water. The Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta, an important source of drinking water for over 20 million Californians, is currently under court ordered mandates to reduce pumping, and is the cause of a spirited debate (and litigation) among stakeholders. Based on its series of levees, scientists have raised the alarm that the current method of managing water in the Delta cannot be sustained in the long term. Other concerns over native fish populations have made the Delta a contentious location. Some regions are trying to solve these issues using alternate methods. In order to maintain crop yields, Central Valley groundwater has been over-pumped, meaning that underground reserves of water are being depleted without a consistent way to refill them. Parts of the landscape are sinking, in some areas by up to two feet per year. Although the state legislature has attempted to prevent this practice, there are still no firm rules about how much water can be pumped. If farmers don’t have water from other sources, they will continue pumping, which can lead to less water for the future. California produces two-thirds of all American fruits and over onethird of all American vegetables, meaning that agricultural issues here affect huge swaths of the country. Usage and payment are one area that most consumers are most familiar with. There has long been underlying tension regarding payment for water. California cities often pay more than agricultural users, meaning that cities essentially subsidize water usage for farming purposes. Some say that this makes sense, as agriculture is predictably a large user of water, using about 80% of all water that goes to businesses and homes. Use in urban areas such as the Bay Area are also a large drain on resources, but as populations have increased, per capita usage has decreased, showing that it is feasible to use water conservation practices. During the last drought, the agriculture industry lost a lot of revenue. Wells dried up and cities implemented water-saving measures. Thousands of trees died, helping to fuel the historic fires of 2020. As the effects from climate change grow more extreme, droughts are going to become more common, and water shortages are likely. These conditions raise questions, such as: who should get to pump groundwater? What do we do when the aquifers run dry? How involved should the state government be? These are all difficult questions, but they need to be answered soon, before the water crisis gets worse. In order to maintain water levels and prepare for the future, state and regional partners must make plans now in order to manage future droughts. This only gives a brief glimpse into the complicated topic that is California water. I encourage you to conduct your own research on the subject, which is as engrossing as it is complex. In Piedmont, there are some things that can be done to reduce individual water usage. • Consumption What you purchase can impact water usage. One cotton t-shirt requires 2,700 liters of water to produce, which is equivalent to about two years of an individual’s drinking water. One pair of jeans can take 7,500 liters of water to produce. In addition to clothing, certain food staples such as wheat and soy that are used to feed cattle and livestock are particularly water intensive. • Indoors Over half of indoor water use comes from the bathroom. Toilets are the highest water user inside the home. Fix leaky toilets and install low-flow. Take shorter showers. • Outdoors Watering landscaping is a huge water user. Use drought-resistant native plants in your yard, and carefully plan the best time to water. Install a rain barrel and use it to water outdoors when possible. This is just a beginning guide to how to save water. There are further resources online to learn more about saving water. You can also use Piedmont’s Climate Challenge website to learn more and work with friends to reduce your water consumption. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. pages.text: Wednesday, June 2, 2021 3 California’s drought crisis By Nate Redinbo Being a California resident requires some degree of drought familiarity. Currently three quarters of the state is experiencing extreme drought. Last year at this time, preceding historic wildfires, 39% of the West was experiencing drought, and now that number is up to 83%. Distressingly, 38% of the West is currently experiencing “exceptional” drought, an event that typically occurs one to two times a century. These grim statistics show that drought has become part of California life, and there is a growing need to deal with the root problems. Effects of drought can range from more intense and fareaching wildfires, to diminished agricultural returns, to increased prices for drinking water. These outcomes are likely to become more common with the advancement of climate change. Water management practices can affect drought impacts. Since 1979, California’s population has doubled, but water infrastructure projects have lagged behind. The State Water Project, one of the largest public water projects in the world, began in the 1950’s and is still being improved upon today. However, many water projects that residents and farmers still rely on were constructed in the 20th century, and now require improvements. Aging infrastructure struggles are compounded by California’s natural precipitation patterns. Partly due to the coastline and inland mountain ranges, California has some of the most variable patterns of rain of any state. Northern California is currently in one of the largest rainfall deficits in modern history. The paltry rainfall can be partly attributed to a La Niña year. Drier conditions are to be expected, but this year is atypical. Humans continue to release greenhouse gases, which can exacerbate naturally occurring weather events such as La Niña. In addition to weather patterns and water infrastructure issues, there are often conflicts over the best way to secure water. The Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta, an important source of drinking water for over 20 million Californians, is currently under court ordered mandates to reduce pumping, and is the cause of a spirited debate (and litigation) among stakeholders. Based on its series of levees, scientists have raised the alarm that the current method of managing water in the Delta cannot be sustained in the long term. Other concerns over native fish populations have made the Delta a contentious location. Some regions are trying to solve these issues using alternate methods. In order to maintain crop yields, Central Valley groundwater has been over-pumped, meaning that underground reserves of water are being depleted without a consistent way to refill them. Parts of the landscape are sinking, in some areas by up to two feet per year. Although the state legislature has attempted to prevent this practice, there are still no firm rules about how much water can be pumped. If farmers don’t have water from other sources, they will continue pumping, which can lead to less water for the future. California produces two-thirds of all American fruits and over onethird of all American vegetables, meaning that agricultural issues here affect huge swaths of the country. Usage and payment are one area that most consumers are most familiar with. There has long been underlying tension regarding payment for water. California cities often pay more than agricultural users, meaning that cities essentially subsidize water usage for farming purposes. Some say that this makes sense, as agriculture is predictably a large user of water, using about 80% of all water that goes to businesses and homes. Use in urban areas such as the Bay Area are also a large drain on resources, but as populations have increased, per capita usage has decreased, showing that it is feasible to use water conservation practices. During the last drought, the agriculture industry lost a lot of revenue. Wells dried up and cities implemented water-saving measures. Thousands of trees died, helping to fuel the historic fires of 2020. As the effects from climate change grow more extreme, droughts are going to become more common, and water shortages are likely. These conditions raise questions, such as: who should get to pump groundwater? What do we do when the aquifers run dry? How involved should the state government be? These are all difficult questions, but they need to be answered soon, before the water crisis gets worse. In order to maintain water levels and prepare for the future, state and regional partners must make plans now in order to manage future droughts. This only gives a brief glimpse into the complicated topic that is California water. I encourage you to conduct your own research on the subject, which is as engrossing as it is complex. In Piedmont, there are some things that can be done to reduce individual water usage. • Consumption What you purchase can impact water usage. One cotton t-shirt requires 2,700 liters of water to produce, which is equivalent to about two years of an individual’s drinking water. One pair of jeans can take 7,500 liters of water to produce. In addition to clothing, certain food staples such as wheat and soy that are used to feed cattle and livestock are particularly water intensive. • Indoors Over half of indoor water use comes from the bathroom. Toilets are the highest water user inside the home. Fix leaky toilets and install low-flow. Take shorter showers. • Outdoors Watering landscaping is a huge water user. Use drought-resistant native plants in your yard, and carefully plan the best time to water. Install a rain barrel and use it to water outdoors when possible. This is just a beginning guide to how to save water. There are further resources online to learn more about saving water. You can also use Piedmont’s Climate Challenge website to learn more and work with friends to reduce your water consumption. The organization is partnering with Daughter Thai Kitchen and Urban Legend Cellars to feature their food and wines in support of local restaurants and wineries, and to raise funds for the association’s upcoming 60th anniversary. articles.text: Piedmont’s newly-formed Housing Advisory Committee held its first public meeting on May 19. An informational report on the community outreach effort was provided by Lisa Wise Consulting within the results of interviews in November 2020 and the citywide fair housing community survey conducted this year. ADUs and alternatives Interviews were conducted over the course of two days in November with 34 individuals. Respondents brainstormed strategies to increase housing production in the city beyond the development of Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), to include rezoning to allow for more multi-family homes, conversion of houses into duplexes or multi-family structures, and deed restrictions to ensure long-term affordability, among others. Respondents in the November interviews listed Blair Park, the city’s tennis courts, Bank of America, Ace Hardware, and deep lots along the Moraga Canyon as opportunity areas where housing production would be feasible. A community survey was open to residents from March 12 to April 15, and a total of 877 responses were received. Survey results found that the majority of residents support the acquisition and rehabilitation of existing buildings for affordable housing, and would like to prioritize housing for Piedmont’s teachers, first responders, seniors and service providers. Residents were also in favor of more streamlined permit approvals. Those who responded to the survey mostly opposed city-sponsored rent subsidies and are not in favor of developing land owned by the city, school district, or religious organizations. The meeting also included a digital poll, where representatives from Lisa Wise Consulting asked participants to choose their preferred architectural style, street frontage and facade among a sampling of multi-family and mixed-use buildings. Funding The survey found that participants support a proposed Transient Occupancy Tax, but oppose a parcel tax. Transient Occupancy Taxes are paid on temporary lodging at hotels, motels, Airbnbs and vacation rentals. Residents also suggested that the city might issue bonds to create more housing, seek grant opportunities, and explore state, federal, or joint-municipal funding. Respondents also supported an increase in sales tax revenue. The next Housing Advisory Committee meeting will be held on June 15 and will serve as another public outreach workshop. The city welcomes residents to participate in upcoming Housing Advisory Committee meetings. Meeting materials are posted at https://www.piedmontishome. org/event/housing-advisory-committee-meeting-sb-2-workshop. The June 15 meeting will be televised on KCOM-TV, the City’s government television station (Channel 27), and will be available to stream on the city’s website.

articles.text: Rodney Wong, Piedmont’s UPS (United Parcel Service) driver for 22 years, has taken a new job with UPS and will no longer be seen driving his regular delivery route in the familiar big brown truck. A familiar face throughout the city, he now works nights in his new position. Wong explained that Piedmont was his favorite route to cover when he was a “floater” for UPS but joked that his colleagues often passed it up when given the opportunity. “It was too much work, they said,” Wong laughed. “But their loss was my gain. I’ve always considered Piedmont a lovely, peaceful space.” Wong said that, although the work could be strenuous and difficult, that he does miss being a driver. He said he will miss the Piedmont community, the many friendly faces and wagging tails that he’s encountered through the years working here. “In all those years, I’ve never missed more than a few days [of work on the route]. I didn’t get a chance to say a permanent goodbye to people in town. I wanted to write a farewell letter, but it was hard,” Wong said. He will continue with his new assignment until the end of next year, when he likely will retire at age 60. Many residents are more familiar with him due to his active participation each year in the AIDS/LifeCycle event, a 545- mile bike ride from San Francisco to Los Angeles. In 2003 he rode for the first time in the cycling event, a fundraiser in the first week of June for the AIDS FounWong has switched positions to a nightly inside assignment. Oakland resident Rodney Wong served as Piedmont’s UPS driver for 22 years. dation. For one week, cyclists pass through communities largely on less-traveled roads, averaging about 80 miles a day. At the end of each day of riding, cyclists arrive at a camp to eat, shower, and rest before riding out again the next morning. Participants - riders and “roadies” - raise money throughout the year prior to the start of the ride. Wong participated in the event for 14 consecutive years and was well known as one of the top fundraisers in Northern California. Wong’s secret of success – raising over $400,000 over the years – was doing it the old-fashioned way. “I liked writing personal fundraising letters, with a donation form and pre-addressed envelopes. I would leave them with my deliveries, and over a few years I was leaving over a thousand with my deliveries,” Wong said with a smile. The response he received from the Piedmont community was immense - leading to an avalanche of donations and sponsorships. “Some ‘regulars’ would contribute every year,” Wong said. “I’m definitely proud of the community for the support they gave me, and that will be one characteristic I will always remember about this city – how giving it is,” he said. Wong made a point each year to publish in the newspaper an invitation for people to donate to the AIDS/LifeCycle organization. At the conclusion of each ride, he also wrote a letter of thanks to the community, letting everyone know how much money they had raised.

articles.text: a wastewater increase of $1.87 per month, after both proposed The East Bay Municipal Utility District (EDMUD) will hold a virtual public hearing on proposed rate increases to water and wastewater service charges on Tuesday, June 8 at 1:15 p.m. A notice was sent by EBMUD to their customers in Piedmont, Alameda, Albany, Berkeley, El Cerrito, Emeryville, Kensington, and Oakland last week. EDMUD is proposing to increase the rates for both its water and wastewater service charges based on its most recent rate models and cost of service studies. Rates would increase over a two-year period, by approximately 4 percent overall on July 1, 2021, followed by another 4 percent increase the next year, July 1, 2022. This is an approximate increase, individual bills may increase by slightly more or less that amount depending on the specific rates and charges that apply to you and how much water you use. The notice mailed to residents provides the example of an average single family customer, who could expect a water rate increase of $5.19 per month, and annual increases have taken effect. A temporary “Drought Surcharge” may be assessed on all potable water use during a declared drought or water shortage. At the date of the mailed notice, EDMUD had not declared a drought; but in the event that a drought occurs, EDMUD will activate the surcharge in addition to other charges. Drought surcharges are calculated to recover costs of providing supplemental water, cost of water-shortage related customer service, and losses of revenue. How to participate in the hearing The public hearing on June 8 will be conducted via Zoom. To participate in the hearing, enter www.edmud.com/rates on your computer, then enter the Zoom Meeting ID (958-6681-4531) and passcode (810650). To participate telephonically, call 1-699-900- 6833 and enter both numbers, Written comments may be mailed before the hearing date to EDMUD, MS 218, PO Box 24055, Oakland, CA 94623-1055.

articles.text: Each spring the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) welcomes new members to its Board of Directors who will help fulfil the 45-year-old organization’s mission to provide sustained financial support to Piedmont schools through fundraising and community engagement. New members on the board this year are: Colleen Allan, Tonya Antonucci, Amber Brumfiel, Francis Hoang, and Jean Takazawa. Colleen Allan co-chaired this year’s Giving Campaign and is looking forward to leading it again next year. She is a brand marketing professional with nearly 20 years of experience at LinkedIn, Clorox and General Mills. She and her husband Brian Payne have three daughters and they moved to Piedmont for the public schools. “The schools are the cornerstone of the Piedmont community,” said Allan. “I am honored to join the PEF Board to help support and strengthen our schools, especially as we navigate the return to school post-pandemic, through academic programming, enrichment offerings and the Wellness Center to help all of our children to flourish.” Tonya Antonucci is an entrepreneur and marketing professional, with leadership stints at Yahoo!, Women’s Professional Soccer, and the Oakland A’s. Tonya and her partner, Tasha Cupp, moved to Piedmont from San Francisco to raise their daughter and son. Antonucci shares “PEF’s mission-based approach and engagement to support Piedmont schools and the broader community is absolutely crucial for sustaining quality public education for every child.” Amber Brumfiel and her husband, Chris, have lived in Piedmont since 2001, and Amber is a member of the City’s Park Commission. Before becoming the mother of three sons (age 8 and 6-year-old twins), she was a commercial real estate litigator in San Francisco. “I feel strongly about PEF’s emphasis on community engagement in its fundraising efforts,” said Brumfiel. “I want to help make people feel excited about supporting our schools and about the sense of community that our schools provide.” Brumfiel’s commitment to Piedmont is illustrated by her past leadership with Spring Fling and the city’s Harvest Festival. Francis Hoang is a Software Engineer at Salesforce and a California native. Francis and his wife, Kim Dao, have been in Piedmont for over 10 years and have three children. Hoang is strongly supportive of the school district’s holistic approach to education. “[It] is not only focused on academics, but also emotional health. The curriculum fosters the love and understanding of music, the arts, and social issues,” he said. “The foundation’s work in the community is what sets us apart and makes Piedmont a truly special place to raise a family.” Jean Takazawa is a professional educator with over 15 years of experience. She is the creator of the Piedmont Affinity Mentoring program that reaches elementary students as well as offering guidance to high school students. Jean and her husband, Tadashi, have two children in Piedmont schools. “We are fortunate to have so many educators in the district focused not only on learning, but on the social-emotional wellbeing of our children. articles.text: The only total lunar eclipse of the year hid a full moon in total shadow early Wednesday morning, May 26. The ideal viewing position was the center of the Pacific Ocean, but Piedmont and the West Coast still experienced full eclipse conditions for 14 minutes, between 4:11 and 4:25 a.m. Night owl Piedmont residents and amateur astronomers took to the streets early in the morning to view the rare occurrence. In the peak eclipse a deep shade of red enveloped the moon. An interesting phenomenon occurs when staring at an unlit moon: the stars directly behind it become visible. As the moon orbits around the night sky, different stars are behind it, but the glare of the moon usually outshines the stars immediately behind it, This glimpse behind the moon is a rarity. The eclipse was classified as a “Super Flower Blood Moon.” A Blood Moon is another name for an eclipses. A Super Moon, or perigean full Moon, happens when a full moon is closest to the earth. A Flower Moon is the full moon when flowers are at their peak bloom. From any one location a total lunar eclipse is only visible every 2.5 years. The last lunar eclipse visible from the Pacific Northwest zone was on January 20, 2019. The next partial eclipse for the Pacific Northwest will be November 18-19 this year, and then not until May 15, 2022. Solar eclipses are even more rare and occur only when the moon obscures the view of the sun. The next one will be an “Annular Solar Eclipse,” where only the outer circle of the sun is visible creating a “ring of fire.” This will occur next week when the sun passes directly over the north pole on June 10. It will not be visible from the Western United States however. The East Coast of North America will have a partial view of the phenomenon, but the best viewing will be from western Europe. articles.text: Educators tell us that there is no more important activity for preparing our children for success as a reader than reading aloud together. And the earlier the better. Research reveals that the benefits of shared reading include: facilitating language-rich exposure and vocabulary development, fostering the development of listening skills, boosting comprehension, and establishing essential foundational literacy skills which will be critical for reading and spelling eventually. Not to mention the fact that story time is a bonding family ritual that can bring closeness, joy and momentary peace to hectic family life. Many children love books and all related activities from the start. However, throughout the past three decades, I have had many parents of toddlers in my office concerned about the child who is not interested in books, despite parents’ repeated efforts. Often these parents are avid readers themselves, which adds to their dismay. My suggestion is this: let’s apply modern principles of neuroscience to maximize the ageold storytime experience. How do we do this? Recent research points to certain neurotransmitters (chemical messengers in the brain) which are particularly involved in learning. Increasing production of these brain chemicals will improve the story time experience. Let’s consider two of these, and how we can maximize them during book reading. Seratonin is the mood regulator. Taking the time to set the mood will increase the serotonin level in the brain, thereby increasing engagement in the activity which follows. Specifically, increased serotonin enhances memory and learning speed. Consider setting the mood by playing some music before jumping in. We may need to focus on increasing the comforting, ritual aspect of storytime. Think about a special, comfortable space, (diming lights, special reading spot, staying up a few minutes later than usual at bedtime), and aesthetically pleasing illustrations. Creating opportunities for back and forth interactions such as line completion (rather than passively listening) can boost the mood by promoting the relationship/emotional and shared elements of the activity. Increased dopamine levels in the brain is related to increased learning and retention. Dopamine is increased when we find an activity rewarding or pleasurable. To increase the rewarding aspect of book reading, praise your toddler (“I like the way you looked at the pictures/listened/ pointed to the pictures/closed the book”). Encouraging and celebrating attempts is your first hurdle in getting a child engaged in the learning activity you have planned. Eventually learning something new is the reward. Choosing high interest books also boosts the pleasure and reward factors. Novelty has also been shown to increase dopamine. Maybe read in the dark with a flashlight once in a while? Maybe sing, whisper or shout certain words? Make up a surprise twist or ending. Read expressively, read slowly, read quickly. Change character voices. So, for the child who does not relish book time, lets boost the mood as well as the positive feedback. I will follow up in April to look at two other important neurotransmitters, and how we can maximize their production to enhance story time in other ways. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail.com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

articles.text: At a virtual event, Senior Awards were announced for 2021 Piedmont High School held its annual Senior Awards ceremony last night, June 1. Although reduced to a virtual event, the same bounty of awards was presented to members of the Class of 2021. In addition to the perpetual awards (see list below), the school handed out 35 departmental awards, ranging from certificates to trophies and plaques. Students are not told which award(s) they will be receiving in advance to heighten the excitement of being surprised by the administrators, teachers, and counselors with the presentation of each award. Each award winner’s distinguishing accomplishments are expounded upon by the faculty presenters. PERPETUAL AWARDS • Susan Kawaichi Diversity Award Presented to Lynnea Bao, Athene La Jeunesse, and Emma Moorhead The award is named for Kawaichi, a former school board member who co-founded the Appreciating Diversity Committee in Piedmont. The award honors students who promote diversity, tolerance, and progress in the school. Athene La Jeunesse worked with Youth Anti-Racism Project and spoke publicly at numerous events promoting diversity. Lynnea Bao worked for equity throughout the community and also excelled in dance and as a choreographer. Emma Moorhead also won the Outstanding Senior in Dance Plaque. • Gail Dryden Community Service Award The award was won by Bridget Bentley and Helena Lowe At the Piedmont senior awards ceremony, Bridget Bentley and Helena Lowe won the Gail Dryden Community Service Award, a perpetual award presented each year to deserving seniors. The plaque is named for former School Board member Gail Dryden. Bridget Bentley has been a staple in the Scouting Community, winning the William J Peterson Youth Leadership Award earlier in the year. Helena Lowe’s accolades span many sectors as well. She volunteered at the Chabot Space and Science Center, and also competed in Robotics. • League of Women Voters Civics in Action Award Piedmont senior Audrey Edel was named winner of the 2021 League of Women Voters Civics in Action award on June 1. Edel, the Senior Class president, demonstrated a commitment to improving the Piedmont and larger communities throughout her four years in school. Edel founded the Teens for Biden Club (now Teens for Democracy) to get the students involved in campaigning for the November elections. She also spearheaded the immensely successful mentorship program between elementary students and high schoolers during the pandemic. • Eric Swart Rachesky Memorial Certificate Piedmont senior Seamus Meagher won the annual Eric Swart Rachesky Award at the Senior Awards ceremony on June 1. Named after the late Eric Swart Rachesky, a Piedmont High School graduate, the memorial award is presented each year to students who make significant academic leaps, overcoming obstacles and hardships along the way. Meagher excelled in both academia and in sports. He was a multi-sport athlete, playing on the football and basketball teams. • Daughters of the American Revolution Good Citizen Award Jenna Kim was announced as the recipient of the DAR Good Citizen Award last night. Kim competed at the national level as a Piedmont Police Explorer, tutored Havens students through the Advocacy for Asian Americans (AAA) club, all while maintaining a high GPA. • Dean Faberman Memorial Prize (Mock Trial) Piedmont senior Anthony Wong was named the recipient of the annual Dean Faberman Memorial Prize. The plaque is awarded to a graduating senior who excels in public speaking and debate. It was created by the Faberman family in memory of their son, a 1979 graduate of Piedmont High who excelled in public speaking. While attending UC Berkeley he was killed by a drunk driver. Wong participated in Mock Trial all four years in high school. As a junior he became the Lead Prosecuting Attorney for the team. As a senior he was Co-captain, prosecution pretrial attorney, and defense attorney, leading the team to first place in the county and advancing to state competition. Wong was also named the class Salutatorian for having the second highest GPA in his class. • Valedictorian Thomas Chu and Samuel Eisenbach will share the award presented the student with the highest grade point average, each a 4.50 weighted GPA. Chu is an AP National Scholar and completed five AP courses and four Honors courses at PHS. Eisenbach won the Excellence in Mathematic plaque and was the winner of a National Merit Scholarship. • Salutatorian Anthony Wong also won the Dean Faberman Plaque and the Outstanding Journalist Award. Wong also served as President of the Advocacy for Asian Americans (AAA) club this year. • ASB Plaque Piedmont High School seniors Grace Davies and Bella Kjellen were awarded the Associated Student Body (ASB) Award at the June 1 Senior Awards ceremony. The plaque acknowledges students who have shown outstanding leadership skills during their time at Piedmont High School. Davies was the ASB President this year, and frequently acted as student representative during School Board meetings. Kjellen was the ASB Vice President and also found time to compete on the Varsity lacrosse and water polo teams.

articles.text: MOCHA- Museum of Children’s Art 221 Broadway LL-49, Oakland 465-8770 Mocha.org/summercamp Summer Day Camps Sign the kids up for a fun art camp at MOCHA this summer. Showcasing Female architects” will be held the week of June 14. Other themes include Sewing, Afrofuturism, Mixed Media, All About Plants and more. The museum is also open for regular admission M-F. Cazadero Music Camp 385 Cazadero Hwy, Cazadero 527-7500 (Berkeley office) Cazadero.org Overnight Band Camp Cazadero Music Camp, the Grandaddy of California summer music camps, delivers the love of music in a nurturing, inspirational environment for young musicians ages 10-18. For over 60 years, Cazadero has provided kids with in-depth music education and summer camp fun. Set on 33 acres near the Russian River, the camp is in a grove of spectacular redwood trees. Cazadero Music Camp is a unique and affordable sleepaway camp less than 2 hours away. Call their Berkeley office for more information. Q-ZAR 2295 Willow Pass Rd, Concord, 521-9663 Q-ZAR.com Laser Tag and Arcade Q-ZAR Laser Tag is back. The laser tag arena has been a kid favorite for decades and is now open on weekends from noon to 8 p.m. for walk-in Laser Tag games. Private sessions may be booked for weekdays by appointment. Waiver forms must be submitted online and a printed receipt brought in in order to play. Q-ZAR also has dozens of retro and modern video games for the enjoyment of everyone. USS Hornet Tours 707 W Hornet Ave, Alameda, 521-8448 uss-hornet.org Aircraft Carrier and Airplane Museum Take the kids for a tour of the historic USS Hornet berthed permanetly as a museum in Alameda. Visit the Hornet’s hangar and flight decks and explore their growing collection of over 15 historic aircraft. Many of the aircraft on board used the Hornet when it was in service between 1940 and 1970. Starting June 4 and through the weekend, the USS Hornet will remember the Battle of Midway and honor those who participated. The Hornet is currently open Saturday and Sunday.

Meagher excelled in both academia and in sports. He was a multi-sport athlete, playing on the football and basketball teams. • Daughters of the American Revolution Good Citizen Award Jenna Kim was announced as the recipient of the DAR Good Citizen Award last night. Kim competed at the national level as a Piedmont Police Explorer, tutored Havens students through the Advocacy for Asian Americans (AAA) club, all while maintaining a high GPA. • Dean Faberman Memorial Prize (Mock Trial) Piedmont senior Anthony Wong was named the recipient of the annual Dean Faberman Memorial Prize. The plaque is awarded to a graduating senior who excels in public speaking and debate. It was created by the Faberman family in memory of their son, a 1979 graduate of Piedmont High who excelled in public speaking. While attending UC Berkeley he was killed by a drunk driver. Wong participated in Mock Trial all four years in high school. As a junior he became the Lead Prosecuting Attorney for the team. As a senior he was Co-captain, prosecution pretrial attorney, and defense attorney, leading the team to first place in the county and advancing to state competition. Wong was also named the class Salutatorian for having the second highest GPA in his class. • Valedictorian Thomas Chu and Samuel Eisenbach will share the award presented the student with the highest grade point average, each a 4.50 weighted GPA. Chu is an AP National Scholar and completed five AP courses and four Honors courses at PHS. Eisenbach won the Excellence in Mathematic plaque and was the winner of a National Merit Scholarship. • Salutatorian Anthony Wong also won the Dean Faberman Plaque and the Outstanding Journalist Award. Wong also served as President of the Advocacy for Asian Americans (AAA) club this year. • ASB Plaque Piedmont High School seniors Grace Davies and Bella Kjellen were awarded the Associated Student Body (ASB) Award at the June 1 Senior Awards ceremony. The plaque acknowledges students who have shown outstanding leadership skills during their time at Piedmont High School. Davies was the ASB President this year, and frequently acted as student representative during School Board meetings. Kjellen was the ASB Vice President and also found time to compete on the Varsity lacrosse and water polo teams. Let me tell you. Being the sister of a senior is a full-time job. I have to make sure that her prom dress looks good on her and approve an after-party outfit. And that’s only the beginning. Let’s just say if I ever have to look at another pair of six-dollar earBut all I need is a dress. My mother insists that I get better shoes for my dress, but I would much rather just wear a pair of white Converse and When I’m with my sister these days, it’s like watching a reality TV show. The level of drama in the two weeks before prom is huge (the Kardashians are probably jealous). There have been endless hours of scrolling to find the right dress that would make my sister look like a queen, years taken off my life to find the perfect necklace that would fit with her outfit, and too many close calls when her boyfriend almost saw the dress (a secret), so I had to turn into a speedster and steer Not that I’m complaining, it’s just that I think that I have gotten wrinkles from all the stress I’ve been going through. I can’t wait for the day of prom when I get to see my sister and her boyfriend see each other for the first time all dolled up and ready I’ll admit that we stalked other girls on social media to see what prom and graduation dresses they would be wearing so that we would know what my sister is up against. For eighth grade girls it’s just a bunch of texting “have you got your dress yet?” or “Do you want to go dress shopping together?” Really, our dress could be anything. But for seniors, the tradition is to wear white. I think that’s not the best idea because white gets dirty way too quickly. Mi hermana is yet to get a dress so the energy surrounding the house is getting more and more frantic. But in a worst case scenario, my mom has a dress she can borrow. But let’s get to the important items. What about the middle school graduation? First of all, we don’t get to have a dance. Eighth graders used to have a boat dance at graduation, but not for class of 2021 because of Covid. (There is rumor that the 8th grade class might have a boat dance in August, but that’s a little late.) So, no worries about a dress for me. All I will do this June is walk across a stage, get a diploma, and listen to my classmates talk. As tradition goes, people get asked to the prom. The prom asks can range anywhere from standing at a locker with a flower and asking the person when they get there or making a sign and surprising your (hopeful) date to the prom, or if you have extra money laying around, renting a plane and attaching in big letters “Go to prom with me”. I helped my sister with her prom ask: we went to Michael’s together and bought all the supplies. It was the cutest thing watching her worry over the poster’s every detail and making sure it was perfect. In the long run we should have used more glue, because we did lose a “u.” Instead of “Will you?” we had “Will yo?,” which was kind of funny, in my opinion. It doesn’t feel real that I’m graduating from middle school, because I still remember the first day of sixth grade when I thought that I was the coolest person ever. But I wish we could have had a real in-person eighth grade year, so my friends and I could have ruled the school. Somehow, the seventh graders took over that role, though no one knows how. But I wouldn’t want to repeat this year – a year spent couped up at home, making unforgettable memories, and the constant threat of a global pandemic looming. I made amazing friends this year that I hope to keep all through high school. The teachers I had this year managed to make online school not terrible, if not exactly enjoyable, but there’s only so much they could do given the circumstances. I am extremely excited to go to high school, no matter how much it scares me. I still can’t comprehend that my role model, idol, and partner in crime (also known is my sister) is going to college in the fall. Because I remember she held my hand when I walked to kindergarten, when she went to middle school, when she played water balloon volleyball in 5th grade, and when she went on her first date. And now she is going to be walking across a stage and getting a diploma that says “Congrats. Get ready to start your life as an adult.” As a younger sister, that’s really hard. I will miss her not being around 24/7 no matter how many times I fight with her. I can’t wait for her to go chase her dreams and hopefully one day catch them. She deserves the world. And I can’t wait for the day she finishes college. I can’t wait for the day she says, “I do”. I can’t wait for the day I become an aunt. So, this is a thank you to an Anonymous Older Sister. Thank you for being the best big sister I could have ever asked for. It truly is the end of an era that I will never forget. articles.text: The music blared, and water balloons flew Thursday May 27 on the PHS campus, as seniors in the Class of 2021 celebrated their last few days on campus with snacks, trinkets, and, of course, water balloons. During lunch break, ASB seniors gave their classmates Krispy Kreme, Otter Pops and Top Dogs to eat, along with reusable straws, wrist bands, and carabiners. “We were celebrating the seniors. It was a free and fun get together to celebrate the end of the year,” said organizer and Senior Class president Audrey Edel Two buckets of water balloons provided the entertainment on a sunny, beautiful day. English teacher Beth Black and ASB Advisor Aaron Barlin stopped by to catch a couple of balloons. Other teachers playfully requested a ceasefire as they walked by with stacks of papers in their arms. Joy resonated on the high school campus, and deservedly so. Seniors had to wait over a year to return to campus this spring and were the last grade to return. Screams of laughter resonated through Piedmont High and the face masks could hardly contain the smiles. The class of 2021 will have its final get together at the graduation ceremony on Friday June 11 at 5:00 p.m. at Witter Field. articles.text: Highlanders remain undefeated in league at 8-0-1 Photos by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s soccer team plays its final match of the season tomorrow, June 3. The Highlanders are currently 8-0-1 with no league losses. Care to take a guess as to which the hottest team in Piedmont is? With a convincing 5-1 win on the road against rivals San Lorenzo last Tuesday, May 25, Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team remains undefeated in league play with an 8-0-1 record. Their final match of the season is tomorrow, June 3 at Hayward. The victory over the Grizzlies last Tuesday came just one day after suffering its only loss of the season to non-league Bishop O’Dowd 2-0 on May 24. “We scheduled O’Dowd and SLZ a day after each other because we wanted to challenge ourselves. San Lorenzo is a massively tough opponent who you can never take lightly,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. Against SLZ, the Highlanders led 2-0 in the first 15 minutes of action with quick goals from Andre Stankiewicz and William Daniel. The Grizzlies went into halftime within striking distance after scoring from a penalty kick in the 27th minute—it marked the first PHS goal allowed to a Shoreline Division team this season. Stankiewicz nearly had a second goal in the 29th minute, but his shot trailed narrowly wide of the left post. Piedmont’s next goal came around five minutes into the second half after being awarded a free kick from 40 yards, where a lob was headed in by Andrew Szerdy – who started the year on Junior Varsity – putting PHS ahead 3-1. Andre Stankiewicz scored an early goal against San Lorenzo for Piedmont’s first score in a 5-1 win. Center back Sawyer Collins scored a goal against San Lorenzo.
articles.title: PHS boys top rivals San Lorenzo, 5-1

articles.text: Greg Gately, generally a quiet kid at school, bellowed in exuberance, a sound that could be heard by spectators at Witter Field on Friday night, and probably by neighbors within a two-block radius. Gately, one of 13 seniors on the lacrosse team and its offensive leader on faceoffs, had just scored the winning goal barely one minute into overtime to lead his team to a thrilling 9-8 victory over rival Bishop O’Dowd. When looking for the best lacrosse in the East Bay, you’d be hard pressed to find a better rivalry than the one between Piedmont and O’Dowd. Piedmont head coach Ryan Price came from O’Dowd three years ago, and he has not lost to his former school since then. Friday’s win came exactly two weeks after a 7-6 victory at O’Dowd – also in overtime – on May 12. Gately’s goal put an exclamation point on a night dedicated to PHS seniors. Running on adrenalin, he was determined to score. Describing the play, Gately explained, “Everyone was gassed. We just had to get it up the field. We got so lucky they messed it up on their possession. pages.text: Wednesday, June 2, 2021 13 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team finished its 2021 season with a third-place finish in the Western Alameda County Conference tournament after defeating Alameda on Saturday, May 29 at the Encinal Pool in Alameda. In the semifinals on Thursday, May 27, the Highlanders suffered a heartbreaking 8-7 loss in overtime to Bishop O’Dowd. “We knew Alameda would use the same defense that Bishop O’Dowd ran on us. The kids have put in a lot of work [this season]. I’m very grateful for the everyone to help make this happen. They’ve been working since December,” said coach John Savage. The high school water polo Staff Photos Max Wagener scored five goals against Alameda and had a goal against Bishop O’Dowd. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team finished its season with a third-place finish at the Western Alameda County Conference (league) tournament at Encinal in Alameda. They defeated Castro Valley 9-3 on Saturday, May 29, and lost 16-6 to Encinal in the semifinals on Thursday, May 27. “We played great defense against Castro Valley. They are good at driving, and we had to play our best. Our girls stepped up and played as a team on defense. Offensively, we had to think outside the box and start driving more. It’s something I’ve wanted to see all season,” said coach Sarah Mooney. It marks a turnaround for the girls’ program, achieving their top performance in the WACC Tournament since Mooney’s senior year at Piedmont High in the fall of 2014 when they finished with a 16-6 record and runner up to Alameda. articles.text: PHS beats Dublin, San Leandro. Oakland HS; loses to O’Dowd, University Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team is wrapping up a busy end to the 2021 season, winning three of their last five games in as many days starting with a critical 94-88 win over Dublin on Tuesday, May 25 at Binks. In a scheduling nightmare, they played Bishop O’Dowd the next day and lost 82-73. They beat Oakland High 75-72 in the Rawlings Gym on May 27, defeated San Leandro 77-66 on Friday, May 28, and lost 75-56 to University in San Francisco on Saturday. May 29. Whew. What a week. The group of games featured matches against top-ranked schools in the area. Currently, MaxPreps.com ranks Dublin as the No. 3 team in North Coast Section, and WestCoastPreps. com listed them as No. 5 in the Bay Area prior to May 25. University and O’Dowd are ranked in the top 10 by both of the online sports groups. Piedmont clearly is in the mix, ranked No. 9 by both MaxPreps and WestCoastPreps. And the Luke Harris has scored 106 points over the five-game stretch. He makes his final appearance at Binks Rawlings Gym this Friday, June 4, against O’Dowd. season isn’t quite over, with three more games in three days starting tonight, Wednesday, June 2. Tonight’s game against Berkeley brings back former Highlanders’ and current Yellowjackets’ coach Mike Hudson to Piedmont. On June 3, PHS travels to Alameda High before closing the season at Binks Rawling’s Gym against Bishop O’Dowd on Friday night, June 4. 94-88 win over Dublin Dublin, a Division 1 program and last year’s runner up in the NCS Open Division, came into Piedmont heralding its high ranking and looking to conclude its season on a high-note. But the Highlanders quickly dashed the Gaels’ hopes. Piedmont led 28-20 at the end of the first period and nearly put the game out of reach at halftime, leading 52-38. Dublin battled back in the second half and cut the deficit to 75-66 by the start of the fourth quarter. They came within one point, but the Highlanders closed out strong to win the high-scoring game, 94-88. PHS players were on fire from 3-point land, hitting 19 of 30 attempts. JoJo Murphy finished with 25 points and six 3-pointers. Standout sophomore A.J. Harris bagged a career-high 24 points, hitting six-of-seven 3-pointers along the way, and older brother Luke Harris had 21 points and two 3-pointers. “We had a big-time win against Dublin. We had contributions from the starters and the bench guys; we shot the lights out. We were 19 of 30 from three; we just couldn’t miss,” said am ecstatic coach Ben Spencer. 82-73 loss to Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont visited Bishop O’Dowd the next day on Wednesday, May 26, and battled to an 82-73 loss. PHS led 25-22 at the end of the first quarter but trailed 42-39 by halftime. O’Dowd extended its advantage to 60-54 by the start of the fourth and finished with an 82-73 victory. The Dragons’ Jarin Edwards was the catalyst with 27 points, all of which came in the paint. “It was a tough game; it was our third game in three days, but no excuses. This one definitely stings, I hope we remember that feeling when the buzzer went off,” said senior captain Luke Harris. Final stats include: Harris with 25 points, three assists, and two steals. Murphy had 24 points, three boards, four assists, and a steal. A.J. Harris had 13, seven rebounds, three assists, two steals. Raydan Holmes had five points, two rebounds, and two steals. 75-72 win over Oakland In another critical matchup, the Highlanders led Oakland High 23-16 at the end of the first Staff Photos Piedmont three of five games in a five-day stretch. They close their season this week with three more games in as many days: hosting Berkeley tonight, at Alameda tomorrow, and home against O’Dowd on Friday. quarter and held a comfortable 41-29 lead by halftime. But the Wildcats scrapped away to cut the deficit to 58-51 by the start of the fourth quarter. Piedmont held onto the lead, but squeaked away with a 3-point win, 75-72. Murphy led with another monster game with 34 points, six boards, four assists, and a steal. Luke Harris finished with 21 points, four rebounds, three assists, and three steals. A.J. Harris had 12 points, eight rebounds, three assists. Holmes had eight points, four boards, one assist, and a steal. 77-66 win over Pirates The Highlanders led San Leandro 17-14 after the first quarter before jumping ahead 39-28 by halftime. The Pirates outscored Piedmont in the third quarter to come within 8 points, 53-45, before Purple and White extended the advantage with 24 points in the final quarter for the 77-66 victory. Murphy remained red hot with 31 points, Luke Harris had 24, A.J. Harris put up eight, Holmes and Zac Evans had four points. 75-56 loss to University Playing their fifth game in five days, Piedmont walked into San Francisco last Saturday for a game with the University Red Devils, among the top-ranked teams in the Bay Area. Playing on weary legs, the Highlanders trailed 23-17 at the end of the first period and 42-27 at halftime. The Red Devils extended the lead to 61-44 by the end of the third before coasting home with the win. Murphy and Luke Harris each were held to 15 points. A.J. Harris had 11, and Parker Terrill had seven points. NEXT UP Piedmont (10-3) plays Berkeley tonight, Wednesday, June 2 at Binks Rawlings Gym at 7:00 p.m. Tomorrow, J, they play at Alameda High at 8:15 p.m., and then end the season in the Piedmont gym on Friday, June 4 against Bishop O’Dowd at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont’s badminton team finished the abbreviated 2021 season with a 4-1 record. The squad opened its season with a 10-4 loss to San Lorenzo on April 29 before reeling off four straight wins – against Hayward 9-6 on Saturday, May 1, Encinal 6-5 on Thursday, May 6, Hayward 9-5 on Saturday, May 8, before a 4-2 win over Tennyson to end the season on Thursday, May 20. The Piedmont High badminton team gathered for a team photo after the end of its season. The Highlanders were forced to suspend activities for two weeks following a positive COVID-19 case on the roster on May 12. It effectively put an end to their once promising season. There was no season-ending league tournament. “The coaches tried [for a league tournament] but the logistics were too difficult. Many of the schools did not have enough players this year. Piedmont was the only team with a full roster,” explained coach David Siu. 4-2 win over Tennyson In its most recent match, Piedmont took nine eligible athletes to Tennyson and came away with a 4-2 win. Linus Lee won at boys’ singles, Jonathan Wu and Dylan Ong won at mixed doubles, Anne-Marie Gibbs won at girls’ singles but Cameryn Kwong lost. At girls’ doubles, August Thigpen and Sally Post won, while Kira Ma and Truc Le lost. Final set scores were not recorded. 9-5 win over Hayward On Saturday, May 8, Piedmont swept boys’ singles, mixed doubles, and took two of three boys’ doubles matches. At boys’ singles, No. 1 starter Collin Mortimer won 21-10, 21-10; Linus Lee won in three sets, 9-21, 21-18, 21-17 at No. 2; Ethan Tran won 21-5, 21-18 at No. 3. To mixed doubles, No. 1 pair of Thomas Yu and Isa Griffis won 21-11, 21-9; No. 2 Jerry Liu and Sam Lee won in three sets, 9-21, 21-19, 21-14; No. 3 Jonathan Wu and Dylan Ong won 21-9, 17-21, 21-7. In doubles, Jeremy Yiu and Niko Rapport won 21-6, 21-8 at No. 1; No. 2 brother pairing of David and Gary Zhou won 21-13, 21-11. 6-5 win against Encinal Piedmont won narrowly 6-5 on May 6 with help of a clean sweep by the three boys’ singles matches in straight sets. At No. 1 Mortimer won 21-7, 21-7; No. 2 Tran won 21-10, 21-8; No. 3 Lee won 21-2, 21-4. In boys’ doubles, No. 1 Yiu and Rapport won 21-6, 21-6; No. 2 the Zhou brothers won 21-1, 21-5; No. 3 Wu and Roman Reyes lost 21-1, 21-5. In mixed doubles, No. 1 Yu and Griffis were the only victorious team 21-5, 21-5. No. 2 and No. 3 scores were not recorded. Encinal lost two girls’ singles and two girls’ doubles matches. In singles, Kwong lost 21-4, 21-6 at No. 1; No. 2 Katie Wen lost 21-5, 21-6. At doubles, Kim and Foo lost 21-15, 21-10 at No. 1; No. 2 Violet Faust and Kira Ma lost 21-9 and had to forfeit the second set. 9-6 win over Farmers On May 1, Piedmont’s 9-6 win featured a sweep of mixed doubles and girls’ doubles, while the boys’ doubles teams won two of three, and boys’ singles took a match. In girls’ doubles, Lucy Filler/ Thigpen won 21-12, 21-19 at No. 1; Kwong/Faust won 21-7, 21-17 at No. 2; Angie Foo/Ma won 21-8, 21-14. The mixed doubles sweep included Thomas Yu/Griffis winning 21-16, 21-3 at No. 1; Liu/Lee won 21-11, 21-19 at No. 2; Wu/ Ong won 21-17, 21-15 at No. 3. In boys’ singles, Linus Lee started at No. 1 to win in comeback fashion: 7-21, 21-18, 22-20. 10-4 loss to SLZ Piedmont’s lone loss, 10-4, came at the hands of San Lorenzo in the season-opener on April 29, Mortimer won at No. 1 singles 21-17, 21-14; Yiu/Rapport won 21-7, 21-4 at No. 1 boys’ doubles; David and Gary Zhou won 21-11, 21-4 at No. 2. The mixed doubles No. 1 pair of Yu and Griffis won 21-9, 21-13; No. 2 Liu/Lee won 21-15, 21-11.

articles.text: The Girls Academy League hosted a Talent Identification event in Northern California on May 24, featuring the top talent in the League’s Northwest conference from the 2004, 2005, 2006, and 2007 age groups. The Girls Academy advertised these events as scouting opportunities for the U.S. Soccer youth national teams. This was the fourth regional event for the 2020- 21 season. Lamorinda led the way among the clubs with 29 players called into the event between the four age groups. FC Bay Area and San Francisco Elite Academy (SFEA) each had 21 players called into the event. Piedmont soccer players on the Lamorinda team selected for the Girls Academy Talent ID Event included Sadie Lahey-Teare (defense) and Audrey Lam (midfield) in the age 2005 division, and defenders Amy Derr and Rina Higashi in the 2006 age division.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) presents an exhibition of the work of Nam June Paik on display now through October. The exhibition presented by SFMOMA is the first-ever West Coast retrospective. It celebrates Paik’s collaborative approach that transcended genres, traditions, and norms, while also highlighting the playful and profoundly radical work he was known for. The exhibition premiered earlier this month and brings together more than 200 works by the experimental artist who has bridged art, music, performance, and technology in groundbreaking ways. The Korean-American artist worked with a variety of media and is considered to be the founder of video art. He is credited with the first use of the term “electronic super highway” to describe the future of telecommunications in 1974. Paik’s influence is still felt in pop culture, music, and film. He passed away in 2006. To obtain tickets and for more information, visit: https://www. sfmoma.org/exhibition/namjune-paik-2021/. returning to the stage this summer, with the premiere of Hold These Truths beginning on June 8 and being performed through July 3. It is the first live event the theatre company has presented in over a year. Directed by Jeanne Sakata and Jeffrey Lo, Hold These Truths is based on the true story of Gordon Hirabyashi. Hirabayashi’s defiance of President Roosevelt’s Executive Order authorizing the incarceration of thousands of Japanese Americans led him into a 50-year journey of advocacy. The play was inspired by many hours of interviews conducted by Sakata with Hirabayashi, as well as anecdotes and primary sources from his life. The New York Times called the play a “gripping story about a shameful chapter of our country’s history,” in its re-telling of the American internment order of 1942. articles.text: presenting drive-in performances ODC Dance Theatre, a post-modern and contemporary dance company based in San Francisco, will kick off a twoweek festival of virtual events beginning tomorrow, June 3. Traditionally, ODC Theatre welcomed patrons to its campus in the Mission District of San Francisco for an array of contemporary dance pieces and performances during the annual “Walking Distance Dance Festival.” This year, re-imagined as an entirely virtual festival and re-named as the ODC Theater Festival, patrons can expect a packed line-up for two weeks of world premieres and film adaptions of previously staged work. The festival will conclude on June 12. Among the highlights will be a world premiere film by ODC Theater Resident Artist Antoine Hunter (Purple Fire Crow), as well as works by NAKA Dance Theater, Catherine Galasso and Dave Cerf, Margaret Jenkins and Rinde Eckert, Geoff and Dan Hoyle, Garrett and Moulton Productions, Robert Moses’ Kin, Hope Mohr and Maxe Crandall, and Monique Jenkinson/Fauxnique. The festival will also feature films by ODC/Dance and the 2021 awardees of the Opportunity Fund at ODC Theater, to include Jeremy Bannon-Neches, Nicole Maria Hoffschneider, and Noah Wang. Visit https://odcdance.org/festival for ticketing information. now through July 3. In the redesigned parking lot at Flax Art at 1501 Martin Luther King, Jr. Way in Oakland. Due to COVID-19 and county restrictions, all performances will be presented as drive-in experiences. Each audience member is required to remain in a fully enclosed vehicle, and performers will be visible to all vehicles, with the show’s soundscape transmitted via FM radio. Restrooms are available. Kathleen Collins’ “Begin the Beguine: a Quartet of One Acts” had its world premiere on May 28, and will be shown through July 3. articles.text: Lily Tomlin and Julie Garner in a scene from Grandma. Don’t be misled by the trailer or the posters for the just-released film, Grandma. This is not a road trip across Nebraska with Lily Tomlin as Elle, the snarky/wise, playing-it-for-laughs grandma. She is accompanied by her clueless, teenage granddaughter, Sage, portrayed by Julia Garner, as the story explores the generational chasm that defines and separates them. As example, when Elle mentions The Feminine Mystique, Sage assumes she’s referring to a character in the X-Men series. But this is a wonderful, character-driven film that was written by director Paul Weitz for Tomlin. Without question her Oscar-worthy performance is a tour-de-force. There is nothing about Elle that is shallow or casually flippant; rather, she is a 70-something woman who is still grieving for the loss of her partner of 38 years, Violet. Elle is also a no-compromise feminist, a poet, and a retired college professor who feels herself falling, incrementally, into a misanthropic well of emptiness. After a hurtful scene at the opening of the film in which she breaks up with a younger woman, Olivia (Judy Greer), calling her a mere footnote in her life, she weeps for all that is now absent. What’s left? Feeling angry and maudlin, dressed in her scholarly cap and gown, she is going through old photographs when the doorbell rings. It’s her granddaughter, Sage, who has turned to her grandmother for help and money. She’s a senior in high school and pregnant and needs $600 for an abortion scheduled for later that day. Sage can’t turn to her mother, Judy (Marcia Gay Harden), who will shower her with rage and criticism. Elle, as it turns out, is also broke (she’s recently sold wind chimes she made out of her credit cards to pay off all of her debts.) Grandmother and granddaughter set out on a kind of L.A. road trip, going to Elle’s old friends and acquaintances to raise the money by that afternoon. The ride? Violet’s vintage Dodge. At every stop, Elle, with Sage in tow, demonstrates that her irascible, foul-mouthed, shortfuse temper may stand her in good stead in keeping the world at bay, but it doesn’t help when it comes to getting cash from those she knows. For those she drops in on, she’s a splinter under a fingernail, a fact demonstrated eloquently in one scene with a longago flame, Karl (Sam Elliot), who has the cash but can’t let go of the hurt Elle caused him 40 years earlier. There is a patina of humor in many of the scenes, including one that is especially funny – a confrontation Elle and Sage have with Sage’s irresponsible, “not my problem” boyfriend. In the main, however, the issues involved, to include the decision to have an abortion, are serious and sad and touching. So many of the films released today merely circle the drain of farce. Grandma is the antidote, and the antithesis. It is filled with honesty and doesn’t back away from the pain felt by Elle as she struggles to come to terms with the hole left in her life by Violet’s illness and death. To spend 38 years with another person, creating a quilt of experiences, stitching days and years into a familiar pattern and then have that person suddenly gone involves regret that can seem insurmountable. Make no mistake, this is a very special film, one that is heartfelt from the first frame until the last. Grandma. Directed by Paul Weitz. Starring Lily Tomlin, Julie Garner, and Marcia Gay Harden. 1 hr., 18 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Grandma a gem of a film with Lily Tomlin

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré The power of fine filmmaking can be extraordinary. Take the issue of illegal immigration, generally regarded in the abstract – our borders are porous, hence there are 11 million undocumented workers in America. It is a problem that is distant, political, a conundrum and one from which we are often insulated. But create an irresistible story about a gardener, Carlos Galindo (Demian Bichir), living in East Los Angeles, without documents, a single parent raising a 16-yearold boy, Luis (Jose Julian), and suddenly the problem becomes real, even personal. At the center of this wonderful film is a principled man, cutting and trimming the grounds of the wealthy, while struggling to keep himself and Luis above water. His goal, his dream, is to have his own truck, his own tools and mower, and so create a life that has at its center, family and stability. A Better Life is a moving portrait of Carlos, who leaves his one-bedroom bungalow each morning at dawn and returns long after dark, falling exhausted onto the hard-used sofa in the living room. He is unaware that his son is drifting away and is finding the faux family security of gangs more inviting than the home offered by his father. Luis, who was born in America, stands with one foot in the culture of his parent and one foot in the culture he finds at school and on the street. His connection to Mexico is tentative, the language and customs seeming ever more strange. Each day Carlos copes with a shroud of anxiety because of his illegal status, ever fearful that he will be stopped by “la migra” and asked for some form of identification. The gardener he works for offers to sell his truck to Carlos and include his client list. He is returning to Mexico. But Carlos, who has no license, no I.D., decides to take the risk. He views the truck as the path to the American dream. Filled with pride, he drives through Los Angeles, looking out the window of the truck. We see parts of the city that are hidden from the usual traveler. There is a diversity created by immigrants that is rich with color and vitality. These are not the mean streets; they are, however, the hardscrabble streets. Sadly, many of the inhabitants, though they contribute to America, are part of a shadow population that is seen but not seen, residing in a place apart, living in immigration ghettos filled with doss-apartments, the drapes tightly closed. But just as Carlos senses that life is about to turn around, events occur that put him and his son in jeopardy. The film is not a political tract or a polemic about immigration. It is a deeply human story, both touching and compelling, about a father and his son who learn about one another as they set about recovering something they have lost. Their journey is transformative. A Better Life. Directed by Chris Weitz. Starring Demian Bichir, Dolores Heredia, Jose Julian, Joaquin Cosio and Tim Griffin. 1 hr., 38 min. Rated PG-13
articles.title: A Better Life a lovely film about an immigrant father and son
