articles.text: A scene from the Dreamworks animation movie, The Croods. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Croods is a comedy of sorts, set in prehistoric times (the Pilocene era). The Croods are a dysfunctional family of five who live in a cave and only venture out to collect food. Otherwise they obey the pater familia, Grug (Nicolas Cage), and remain safely inside, living by his motto, “Never not be afraid.” They are prey and their world is filled with predators. The Croods – mother, Ugga (Catherine Keener), Gran (Cloris Leachman), and brother Thunk (Clark Duke) – are introduced to us in voice over by teenage daughter Eeep (Emma Stone), who is rebelliously curious about what there is to discover beyond the cave. One night, with everyone asleep, she sneaks out, and seeing a strange light in the distance, she investigates. Holding a torch is an evolved Sapien named Guy (Ryan Reynolds), who has discovered fire. He is adventurous, a bit dashing, and relies on intelligence rather than brute force. He looks down on the Neanderthals. Guy warns Eep that an apocalypse is about to happen, likely in the form of lava producing earthquakes, and she and her family should leave their cave for higher ground. When Guy and Eep share this prediction with Grug, he is doubtful and resistant – until their cave is destroyed by a quake. The family is now forced to head out in search of new shelter. Guy leads them into new environs where they encounter a surprising number of critters. He invents things along the way, such as, well, footwear. The plot involves a series of adventurous detours, kind of a Paleolithic road trip in which they discover a bucolic jungle and animals such as saber toothed housecats and a flock of razor-toothed birds. Eventually they do find a cave that is suitable for the family, but by now they have unexpectedly discovered that they prefer to live outside. The Croods, released eight years ago in 2013, was nominated for an Oscar for Best Animated Feature film and was also nominated for a Golden Globe for its dazzling animation. The Croods. Directed by Kirk DeMarco, Chris Sanders. Dreamworks animation. With voices of Nicolas Cage, Emma Stone, & Ryan Reynolds. 1 hr., 31 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: The Croods – welcome to a Paleolithic road trip

articles.text: In an article in the New York Times Magazine, director Spike Jonze, when discussing his film, Where the Wild Things Are, said, “Everything we did, all the decisions that we made, were to try to capture the feeling of what it is to be 9.” While it is true that a movie targeting young filmgoers must engage their imaginations and emotions, it shouldn’t necessarily mirror what it feels like to be 9 years old. At least not completely. There must also be magic and surprise. In other words, a film of this type will find more success if it’s a fable that asks young audiences to suspend their disbelief and climb onboard. It’s something they are fully prepared to do – say, at the drop of a hat. But first, consider the book. Written by Maurice Sendak and published in 1963, it has sold 19 million copies worldwide, including 10 million in the U.S. Its success begs the question, what is there about this story that young readers so completely embrace? The story, after all, comprises only 338 words; 41 lines of text; and is only 37 pages long. Perhaps it’s the fact that story is a seamless melding of reality and fantasy. A boy, Max, dressed in a wolf costume, consumed with a riptide of emotion, rebels, causing mischief, and is sent to his room. And that’s when the magic begins. His room grows into a forest, and he finds a boat and sails to a distant shore where he discovers a band of feral monsters – large, furry, exotic, all strange hybrid animals. He becomes the king of the monsters, wears a crown, carries a scepter, and is empowered. It’s an overwhelming feeling for Max. He stands and yells to the monsters that it’s time to howl and experience their inner wildness. Eventually, however, he decides to return to his family, to those who love him most. Where the Wild Things Are is an elegant and simple story, wonderfully illustrated by Sendak, and one that would appeal to any youngster who feels conflicted and perhaps frustrated at being buffeted by the whims of family, school and siblings, wishing only for a magic place where he or she can be king. In the first act of the film, Jonze captures, with pitch-perfect insight, the existential pain of any kid who feels overwhelmed by life. Max (Max Records) is coping with the divorce of his parents. His sense of isolation is so complete that he talks to fences as if they could talk back. When Max discovers his mother has invited a strange man over for dinner, and sees then nuzzling on the couch, he acts out, argues with his mother and runs from the house, angry and conflicted. It’s at this point that Sendak’s fable begins. And therein is the real challenge for Jonze as a screenwriter. The difficulty of adapting Sendak’s story to the screen is that it lacks even a semblance of a strong narrative arc. There is only a paper-thin plot; there is no real conflict and no resolution. Hence, for Sendak’s book to be adapted to the screen as a 98-minute feature, Jonze had to embellish considerably. But if he deviated too far from the fable template (and from Sendak’s book), he would do so at his peril. Kids wish to be swept up in a story that involves a journey akin to that found in Shrek or Harry Potter or Spy Kids, one in which the protagonist struggles to overcome adversity, achieves a specific goal, is victorious, and in a tale that ends with a nice moral. Jonze’s film draws very little from that recipe. Though the film is imaginative, and the photography superb, the tones are sepia and dark in contrast to the crisp, bright colors of most kids’ movies. In fact, it could be argued that Where the Wild Things Are is not a film intended for children, but for adults who enjoy watching movies that remind them of their childhood. The monsters, which Jonze develops, have names and speak, something they don’t do in the book. They are somber and dysfunctional, and Carol (James Gandolfini), the wild thing Max comes to know best, is given to bouts of scary temper, threatening to hurt Max – even suggesting that Max should be eaten. In the end, there is no emotional center to the film. Even the relationships between the wild things seem too subtle and strange, something that will be missed by the younger audience. It’s clear that Jonze made an astonishing effort to adapt a book that simply did not have enough substance to be made into a feature film. It was a high-risk gamble by the studio and Jonze and is laudable. But is it high gain? Where the Wild Things Are. Starring Catherine Keener, Max Records, James Gandolfini, Catherine O’Hara, Forest Whitaker and Chris Cooper. Directed by Spike Jonze. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG. Max Records stars in Where the Wild Things Are.
articles.title: Where the Wild Things Are – Sendak’s book on the big screen

The Croods – mother, Ugga (Catherine Keener), Gran (Cloris Leachman), and brother Thunk (Clark Duke) – are introduced to us in voice over by teenage daughter Eeep (Emma Stone), who is rebelliously curious about what there is to discover beyond the cave. One night, with everyone asleep, she sneaks out, and seeing a strange light in the distance, she investigates. Holding a torch is an evolved Sapien named Guy (Ryan Reynolds), who has discovered fire. He is adventurous, a bit dashing, and relies on intelligence rather than brute force. He looks down on the Neanderthals. Guy warns Eep that an apocalypse is about to happen, likely in the form of lava producing earthquakes, and she and her family should leave their cave for higher ground. When Guy and Eep share this prediction with Grug, he is doubtful and resistant – until their cave is destroyed by a quake. The family is now forced to head out in search of new shelter. Guy leads them into new environs where they encounter a surprising number of critters. He invents things along the way, such as, well, footwear. The plot involves a series of adventurous detours, kind of a Paleolithic road trip in which they discover a bucolic jungle and animals such as saber toothed housecats and a flock of razor-toothed birds. Eventually they do find a cave that is suitable for the family, but by now they have unexpectedly discovered that they prefer to live outside. The Croods, released eight years ago in 2013, was nominated for an Oscar for Best Animated Feature film and was also nominated for a Golden Globe for its dazzling animation. The Croods. Directed by Kirk DeMarco, Chris Sanders. Dreamworks animation. With voices of Nicolas Cage, Emma Stone, & Ryan Reynolds. 1 hr., 31 min. Rated PG. A Scene from Spike Jonze’s Where the Wild Things Are. Where the Wild Things Are – Sendak’s book on the big screen By Chris Honore’ In an article in the New York Times Magazine, director Spike Jonze, when discussing his film, Where the Wild Things Are, said, “Everything we did, all the decisions that we made, were to try to capture the feeling of what it is to be 9.” While it is true that a movie targeting young filmgoers must engage their imaginations and emotions, it shouldn’t necessarily mirror what it feels like to be 9 years old. At least not completely. There must also be magic and surprise. In other words, a film of this type will find more success if it’s a fable that asks young audiences to suspend their disbelief and climb onboard. It’s something they are fully prepared to do – say, at the drop of a hat. But first, consider the book. Written by Maurice Sendak and published in 1963, it has sold 19 million copies worldwide, including 10 million in the U.S. Its success begs the question, what is there about this story that young readers so completely embrace? The story, after all, comprises only 338 words; 41 lines of text; and is only 37 pages long. Perhaps it’s the fact that story is a seamless melding of reality and fantasy. A boy, Max, dressed in a wolf costume, consumed with a riptide of emotion, rebels, causing mischief, and is sent to his room. And that’s when the magic begins. His room grows into a forest, and he finds a boat and sails to a distant shore where he discovers a band of feral monsters – large, furry, exotic, all strange hybrid animals. He becomes the king of the monsters, wears a crown, carries a scepter, and is empowered. It’s an overwhelming feeling for Max. He stands and yells to the monsters that it’s time to howl and experience their inner wildness. Eventually, however, he decides to return to his family, to those who love him most. Where the Wild Things Are is an elegant and simple story, wonderfully illustrated by Sendak, and one that would appeal to any youngster who feels conflicted and perhaps frustrated at being buffeted by the whims of family, school and siblings, wishing only for a magic place where he or she can be king. In the first act of the film, Jonze captures, with pitch-perfect insight, the existential pain of any kid who feels overwhelmed by life. Max (Max Records) is coping with the divorce of his parents. His sense of isolation is so complete that he talks to fences as if they could talk back. When Max discovers his mother has invited a strange man over for dinner, and sees then nuzzling on the couch, he acts out, argues with his mother and runs from the house, angry and conflicted. It’s at this point that Sendak’s fable begins. And therein is the real challenge for Jonze as a screenwriter. The difficulty of adapting Sendak’s story to the screen is that it lacks even a semblance of a strong narrative arc. There is only a paper-thin plot; there is no real conflict and no resolution. Hence, for Sendak’s book to be adapted to the screen as a 98-minute feature, Jonze had to embellish considerably. But if he deviated too far from the fable template (and from Sendak’s book), he would do so at his peril. Kids wish to be swept up in a story that involves a journey akin to that found in Shrek or Harry Potter or Spy Kids, one in which the protagonist struggles to overcome adversity, achieves a specific goal, is victorious, and in a tale that ends with a nice moral. Jonze’s film draws very little from that recipe. Though the film is imaginative, and the photography superb, the tones are sepia and dark in contrast to the crisp, bright colors of most kids’ movies. In fact, it could be argued that Where the Wild Things Are is not a film intended for children, but for adults who enjoy watching movies that remind them of their childhood. The monsters, which Jonze develops, have names and speak, something they don’t do in the book. They are somber and dysfunctional, and Carol (James Gandolfini), the wild thing Max comes to know best, is given to bouts of scary temper, threatening to hurt Max – even suggesting that Max should be eaten. In the end, there is no emotional center to the film. Even the relationships between the wild things seem too subtle and strange, something that will be missed by the younger audience. It’s clear that Jonze made an astonishing effort to adapt a book that simply did not have enough substance to be made into a feature film. It was a high-risk gamble by the studio and Jonze and is laudable. But is it high gain? Where the Wild Things Are. Starring Catherine Keener, Max Records, James Gandolfini, Catherine O’Hara, Forest Whitaker and Chris Cooper. Directed by Spike Jonze. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG. Max Records stars in Where the Wild Things Are.

articles.text: Live theater returned to Piedmont High School from May 21 to 23 with four sold-out performances of the musical Mamma Mia! The performances were held in the amphitheater on the high school campus, with standard Covid health precautions in place. Virtual auditions were held last September, and the cast rehearsed 100% remotely for six months. In-person rehearsals began less than one month before the show’s opening. In a curtain speech before each performance, Director and choreographer Amy Moorhead expressed gratitude to the cast and crew for their “trust in each other, and their trust in the process of putting on a musical in extremely uncertain times.” The show included 22 students: Ellie Andersen, Aaron Belikoff, Lucca Carr-Veramo, Nellie Daniels, Sophia Ethington, Cole Garcia, Alex Guevara, Shari Lynn Halden, Maya Hollingsworth, Charlie Lucas, Scott McKenzie, Graham McWeeny, Photos by Julie Reichle Shari Lynn Halden in the lead role in Mamma Mia. Molly McWeeny, Emma Moorhead, Payton Morell, Quincy Munyan, Corinn Richards, Zoe Saldanha, Katherine Stormer, Gabe Symkowick, Holden Temple, and Aidan Weiss. The production was directed by Moorhead, with vocal direction by Jon Gallo, and PHS vocal music teacher Jorell Chavez. Zoe Saldanha (left), Emma Moorhead, and Payton Morell in Mamma Mia. Quincy Munyan (left), Cole Garcia, and Lucca Carr-Veramo in Piedmont High School’s production of the musical Mamma Mia.

articles.text: Henry Fisher, a dapper Hollywood violinist, with his luxurious and speedy Auburn automobile, a purchase influenced by a friend, famous racecar driver Barney Oldfield. The Indianapolis 500 was celebrated last Sunday. The Bay Bridge on Tuesday evening seemed like a warm-up to the race. The posted speed limit on the Bay Bridge is 50 miles an hour. Cars going 60 miles an hour were cowering in the right lane. All around them, people were driving like lunatics, weaving in and out and going between 75 and 80 miles an hour. It was a very harrowing experience. Was it, perhaps, the lunar eclipse? Speaking of speed demons, I am reminded of one of the most interesting characters in the history of automobile racing. He was a cigar-chomping former bicycle racer named Barney Oldfield. In his day, Oldfield was synonymous with speed itself. Cops would pull over speeders and say to them: “Who do you think you are, Barney Oldfield?” I don’t know if Barney Oldfield played the violin or was even interested in music. But I do know that he had a big influence on my first violin teacher. It was because of Oldfield that my first violin teacher fell in love with fancy cars. Included among these were cars by Stutz, Auburn, and Cord. The great Italian opera composer Giacomo Puccini was also in love with fast cars. His passion for speed almost resulted in his death in a serious car crash. Puccini wasn’t the only one. Immortal violinist Jascha Heifetz also had a passion for cars. He wasn’t addicted to speed in the same way that Puccini was, but he used to drive his Bentley like a parking lot attendant. Heifetz was concerned about the air that we breathe, and he commissioned the father of a friend of mine to build a special electric car which he publicized in every way. He was also responsible, in large part, for the emergency number 911. Thank you, Jascha. Another violinist interested in fancy cars was the Jan Kubelik, a Czech. He used to drive around in a Duesenburg. For effect, he strapped his famous Stradivarius to the side of the car where the spare tire usually went. Kubelik loved California so much that he bought a house in Los Gatos and was a frequent guest at the Bohemian Grove. Kubelik’s successor was a guy named Vasa Prihoda. His passion was big and powerful Mercedes-Benz convertibles. He was equally adept in virtuoso violin playing and virtuoso driving. There was even talk that he might become a racecar driver. The old days certainly had some interesting characters. They were great musical personalities and they knew how to enjoy life. It has been my great pleasure to write about music education and to advocate music as core curriculum. One of the best examples of making music fun is the song “When the Saints Go Marching In. “See if you can find the duet version as sung by Louis Armstrong and comedian Danny Kaye. In about three minutes you get an introduction to music and learn the names of almost every famous composer. Armstrong and Kaye are having a great time and so will every listener. It has my highest recommendations.
articles.title: Lunatics, speed demons, and musicians

articles.text: The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations, the “Indie Next List,” from independent booksellers. The titles below are accompanied by reviews from bookstore owners from across the country. For full book reviews, and ways to support small bookstores, visit: www.indiebound.org/indienext-list Morningside Heights, by Joshua Henkin was named one of 2021’s most highly anticipated new books by Newsweek Morningside Heights Fiction “I loved this book! The writing is beautiful, and the character development is phenomenal. I was moved by all of the characters in the story, but quirky Arlo stands out as a favorite. I also shed a few tears, so this book has it all. It’s a winner with so much heart! I highly recommend it.” —Sarah Fox, Titcomb’s Bookshop, East Sandwich, MA Malibu Rising lantine Books, Fiction “This ode to Malibu in the 1980s is the perfect beach read. Four famous siblings throw a star-studded party and over the course of 24 hours find their lives changed forever. It’s enthralling and layered and so vivid it could be a memory. Perfectly paced and suspenseful from page one!” —Meagan Dallner, Books Are Awesome, Parker, CO The Other Black Girl Books, Fiction “This is the tale of two Black women coworkers in the cutthroat publishing industry trying to determine if they are friends or enemies. A literary fiction tale with a side of suspense, this expertly woven critique on society is bound to keep readers on the edge of their seats.” —Kirsten Wilson, The Snail on the Wall, Huntsville, AL One Last Stop tin’s Griffin, Fiction/Romance “What a magical and creative tale; an addictive read that I did not want to put down. A fun and diverse cast of characters took this story to the next level. With such wide appeal, I know I will be able to put One Last Stop into the hands of almost any customer this summer.” —Cori Cusker, Bright Side Bookshop, Flagstaff, AZ Animal Press, Simon & Schuster, Fiction “Much like Taddeo’s Three Women, this novel is not for the prudish or for people who like their women to be silent or demure. If you are looking for originality, sexiness, or fearlessness in your next read, this is the book for you. Grab the reins and be prepared for a ride!” —Shane Mullen, Left Bank Books, St. Louis, MO Legends of the North Cascades quin Books, Fiction “A sad, sweet, and ultimately hopeful novel of loss, family, and wilderness. Even while maneuvering through two very different story lines, Legends of the North Cascades is imaginative, endearing, and poignant. This is my new favorite of Evison’s novels.” —Stephen Sharpe, A Book for All Seasons, Leavenworth, WA The Maidens Books, Fiction/Thriller “Alex Michaelides approaches The Maidens with a skillful hand and an eye for the mystery/thriller novel while expertly intertwining dark academia and psychological influences. This is one that will keep you invested until the very end.” —Maxwell Leaning, Paragraphs Bookstore, Mount Vernon, OH Unsettled Ground Books, Fiction “Another fantastic story from Claire Fuller, whose novels are full of depth and insight. Unsettled Ground reveals a complex relationship between a mother and her twin adult children, and the secrets that push them to the very edge of existence. I can’t recommend her enough!” —Julie Slavinsky, Warwick’s, La Jolla, CA The Soulmate Equation Books, Fiction “I finished this in one sitting and my neck is killing me. I loved this new story from Christina Lauren, from the third-person point-of-view to the mix of science and romance! It was perfect, from every last side character to the sexual tension between the mains.” —Blair Boles, Beausoleil Books, Lafayette, LA The Thousand Crimes of Ming Tsu Company, Fiction “A raucous romp through a nearly lawless post-Civil War American West. Ming Tsu’s story is captivating and impossible to put down; the cast of characters is just too unique to forget or dismiss. A blood-crusted gem of a tale.” — Jamie Fiocco, Flyleaf Books, Chapel Hill, NC House of Sticks “This timely book follows the life of a young woman whose family immigrates to New York from Vietnam. It is a heartbreaking look at the challenges in overcoming PTSD, poverty, and mental illness. Ultimately, Ly Tran’s story is one of hope, one that is much-needed today.” —Alecia Diane Castro, Sweet Home Books, Wetumpka, AL The Chosen and the Beautiful tion/Fantasy “What would you give up to have it all? Magical and queer as hell, Jordan Baker takes readers through Jazz Age New York as her snark, rage, and feelings for Daisy keep us turning pages until early morning. Like one of Gatsby’s cursed parties, this book was one I wanted to never end.” —Abby Rice, The Briar Patch, Bangor, ME Heaven Editions, Fiction “I loved this book. Its portrayal of bullying is moving and intelligent. Kawakami gives us characters who speak to the heart and illustrate in one form or another the dilemma facing everyone in adolescence. Hopeful but chilling in equal measures.” —Don Luckham, The Toadstool Bookshop, Keene, NH The Kingdoms bury Publishing, Fiction/Fantasy “What a strange, unputdownable book. The Kingdoms weaves characters freed from time and space and memory, rebuilding our world as we know it and inviting us into a delicious story of love and loss.” —Hannah Oxley, Mystery to Me, Madison, WI One Two Three and Co., Fiction “I absolutely loved this heartwarming story of three courageous sisters fighting for justice in their town. It’s a modern David and Goliath tale of small-town America told with wit and heart. Frankel is a superb storyteller, and I did not want my time with this wise and endearing family to end.” —Shannon Burgess, The Bookstore of Glen Ellyn, Glen Ellyn, IL Our Woman in Moscow Morrow, Fiction/Historical “Ruth Macallister runs a New York modeling agency, while twin Iris Digby chooses marriage and motherhood, but her diplomat husband turns out to be a spy. Can Ruth extricate Iris from exile in Moscow? A wonderful plot weaves around Red Scare events of the early 1950s.” —Clay Belcher, Signs of Life, Lawrence, KS Palace of the Drowned Books, Fiction/Thriller “Bridging the gap between genre and literary fiction with enormous skill and agility, Mangan has again given us an electrifying yarn full of menace and atmosphere. With a mesmeric sense of place, Palace of the Drowned is a fully transportive experience.” —Wesley Minter, Third Place Books, Lake Forest Park, WA

articles.text: Come join your friends at the Piedmont Center as it begins to reopen for public events after a year of closure due to COVID-19. LAST WEEKEND - SPRING CREATIVE This is the last weekend to view Spring Creative, an art exhibit by five Piedmont artists at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The gallery will be open from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday, June 5 and 6. The artists exhibiting are Mike Welch, Paula Valenzuela, Valerie Corvin, John Schleuning, and Brian Molyneaux. Artists will be on-site during the final weekend hours to answer questions. Advance reservations are not required. Entry to the exhibition will be through the front doors of the Center at 801 Magnolia Avenue. • • • • • Mike Welch – Large scale oil and mixed media paintings (mikewelchfineart.com) Paula Valenzuela – Mixed media (www.paulavalenzuelaart.com) Valerie Corvin – Painting and mixed media (www.valeriecorvin.com) Jon Schleuning – Watercolor and handmade inks (jonschleuningart.com) Brian Molyneaux – Photography (www.BrianMolyneaux.com) To view a sampling of past exhibits and performances, click on https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d3q9otV5emI

articles.text: Mountain Music, a music store on Piedmont Avenue owned by Piedmont resident and musician Adam Lipansky, never got to hold its grand opening due to the pandemic. Now that many restrictions have been lifted, it will be having its official Grand Opening on Sunday, June 20. The celebration will be a block party, with live music, raffles, food, and vendors. Come join the fun and festivities on Sunday June 20 from 12:00 to 4:00 p.m. Mountain Music is located at 4444 Piedmont Avenue, between J. Miller Flowers and Mountain View Cemetery. For more information call 655-2263 (mountainmusicstore.com).

Basically, there are six main interrelated design disciplines involved. This work is done by hired professionals on projects like large new homes or the new Piedmont high school buildings, or in the case of small remodel jobs, by contractors or homeowners themselves many times, following the standardized building code requirements, as well as city regulations. All development starts with the field of Planning, which involves design and regulatory requirements at the broadest scale. This work ends up in documents like general plans, zoning documents or design guidelines and forms the basis of the design process for all participating professions. When we submit for building permits, applications are first reviewed by the planning department for compliance and then passed on to the building department for more detailed engineering and code checking. Next is Urban Design, which we have addressed in previous columns. It is a narrower scale consideration, somewhere between Planning and Architecture. Difficult to codify, design guidelines come closest to setting the requirements for this invaluable work. There are urban design specialists but architects and landscape architects also support and contribute to this field. Architecture, of course, is the work of buildings themselves – the scale and discipline with which most people are familiar. Architects, usually known for the design of buildings, have traditionally also led, managed, and coordinated the team of professionals from these disciplines whose expertise is needed to deal with all the different specialty issues involved. Landscape Architecture is a discipline whose scope of work is essential and connected to everything, from huge master plans through Urban Design, and down to individual small homes. Like Urban Design, good Landscape Architecture is critical to the success of any project. but unfortunately is not always given the importance required. Interior Design is the discipline most personal to all of us because we see this work up close. Every day we reach out and touch and use the furniture, fixtures, equipment –everything on the inside of the building – that interior designers specify and design. Engineering is a separate layer coordinated with everything that architects, landscape architects and planners design. For retaining walls to not tip over, or sewage systems to have the required capacity, they must be engineered. Unlike small residential projects, the list of engineers involved on larger projects can be long and comprehensive, including those in less known fields like life safety, telecommunications and energy systems. Next: The Aesthetic of Materials Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com LANDSCAPE ARCHITECTURE: In addition to planting, landscape architects’ work includes hardscape (paving) irrigation, monuments, plazas, fountains, fences, trellises – in short, everything outside the building. INTERIOR DESIGN: Besides furniture selection or design, artwork, and surface coverings, interior designers work closely with architects to design and/or specify the materials, textures, colors and finishes of everything from light fixtures to building hardware. ENGINEERING: Engineers’ drawings are the most detailed and specific since they are responsible for the “nuts and bolts” of construction. articles.text: Chicken Curry Stir-Fry an easy, casual dinner for summer nights. This quick stir-fry is inspired by a recent dinner with friends. I prepared a veggie-only side dish of stir-fried zucchini and cherry tomatoes for our alfresco gathering. It made an easy switch to a weeknight dinner by adding chicken for an all-in-one skillet meal. The “weeknight” in the recipe title translates to fast and easy. Using a prepared curry powder blend provides most of the flavor and marinating the chicken pieces beforehand is purely optional. I keep a few varieties of curry powder blends on hand; each has a distinct flavor profile. There are common ingredients – cumin, coriander, turmeric – but each blend brings a nuance to the part of the world that inspired the blend. Stir fry dishes are easily adapted with substitutions. Any combination of meat and vegetables will work. For best results, remember the idea is to slice the meat and vegetables so they will be of similar size for even cooking. Weeknight Chicken Curry Stir-Fry INGREDIENTS • 1-1/2 pounds boneless chicken, sliced into 1-inch pieces • 1 pound tender zucchini, about 5 - 6 young squash, sliced into 1-inch pieces • 15 cherry tomatoes • 1/2 white onion, diced in 1/2” - 3/4” pieces • 2 - 3 teaspoons curry powder • Salt and cayenne pepper, to taste • 2 - 3 teaspoons ghee or vegetable oil that will withstand high heat, divided • Cilantro to garnish INSTRUCTIONS Use a heavy, 12-inch frying pan. Heat the pan over medium-high heat for about one minute. Add 1 teaspoon of ghee or oil and distribute it evenly using a spatula. Add the zucchini in a single-layer, cut-side facing down. Allow to brown slightly, then turn the pieces over to cook on both cut sides. Take care to just barely cook through; this should take only 4-5 minutes. Remove the zucchini to a plate and set aside. With the heat still set at medium-high, add the onion and spread into one even layer. Add a bit of ghee or oil if needed, but there should be enough in the pan so they will not stick. Cook the onion until brown at the edges but are still barely cooked through, then remove from the pan to the plate along with the zucchini. Return the pan to the medium-high heat and wait about one minute to assure the pan is hot. Add the chicken pieces all at once to the hot pan and begin spreading into one layer as quickly as possible. Once the chicken is in one layer, leave it alone to brown; about 5 minutes. Flip the pieces of chicken over and spread them back into a single layer. Add the curry powder and cook another 5 minutes until the chicken is nearly done. Add the cherry tomatoes, cooked zucchini, and onions to the pan with the chicken and stir to combine everything. Cook another 3 or 4 minutes to ensure the chicken is thoroughly cooked and the vegetables are hot. Ideally the zucchini will retain a bit of crunch when bitten. Remove to a serving dish. Sprinkle liberally with chopped cilantro and/or sliced green onions. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

articles.text: Michèle Stone of Oakland, the life partner of Harry Howe, passed away peacefully in her sleep early in the morning of Saturday, May 15, 2021, at Kaiser Oakland Medical Center. She was 78. Born Michèle Dee Hyman in Santa Monica on July 14, 1942, she was the daughter of Frank and Yetta Hyman. Frank was an engineer and moved to various major jobs in Southern California, so she spent her early years in Los Angeles, Mojave, Twenty-nine Palms, Van Nuys, and Pomona before moving to a home in Claremont that her father had designed. After graduating from Claremont High School in 1960, she moved to the Bay Area, where she earned a Bachelor’s degree with a Decorative Arts major at UC Berkeley in 1964. She earned a lifetime teaching credential and first taught with Oakland Unified School District in 1966. She taught first- and second-grade classes in several different schools and managed to earn a Master’s in Education degree from Cal State Hayward. She taught at Crocker Highlands Elementary School for the last 34 years of a 42-year teaching career. The wonderful, full life that Michèle was able to build and enjoy in Oakland included a deep and constant commitment to the community and its future growth and well-being, as evidenced by her influence on the hundreds of children she taught with such dedication and satisfaction. Her membership for many years at Oakland’s Temple Sinai resulted in many lasting friendships spanning all walks of life, while providing her with emotional security and support whenever needed. She spent many years also as an active member of Women’s American ORT, helping The Piedmont Center for the Arts and other performing arts organizations lost one of the principal cheerleaders and supporters with the passing of Michèle Stone on May 15. to support a world-wide network of schools for both children and adults, and was instrumental in the establishment and operation of a local thrift store supporting both her temple and ORT. Michèle also had a deep love of the arts and performing arts and recognized the singular value they provide to communities. She was a collector of books and objects of visual and creative arts of all kinds. She was a supporter and subscriber of Oakland Symphony since the days when Calvin Simmons was its director, and was a moving force supporting the Symphony’s educational and outreach programs, donating hundreds of hours every season. She also was a strong supporter and constant volunteer with Piedmont Center for the Arts, where she typically was the first person in the front row for nearly all concerts. She and Harry were also longtime supporters of and regular attendees at concerts of the New Century Chamber Orchestra, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, the Philharmonia Baroque, Berkeley Symphony, and the SFJazz Center. Michèle loved the excitement of exploring new places and new ideas, traveling extensively and frequently throughout the United States, and throughout Western Europe and the Mediterranean and Aegean Sea areas. She always came home with new friends with whom she stayed in touch over the years. Wherever she went she would be greeted by young adults who had at one time been her students in their first years of elementary school, or adults whose children she had taught. When she was at home, she loved to explore new recipes, to cook for and entertain her many circles of friends, to work on and cherish her rose garden and extensive collection of orchids, and to play mah-jongg and socialize with those with whom she was closest. After all these years of giving, her final gift was to donate her remains to the UCSF Willed Body program, with the hope that she might thus contribute one day to a better outcome for another person, and at the same time relieving her surviving family members from the tasks involved with a funeral or burial. This final gift also relieves all who knew her from any obligation to travel to a specific location in order to visit her spirit, which will instead always be with all those she knew wherever you are. Gifts in memory of Michèle Stone may be made to Oakland Symphony, George Mark Children’s House, or Temple Sinai in Oakland. Michèle is survived by her life partner Harry Howe, her younger brother Steven Hyman, her son Adam, his wife Eran and daughter Emma, and her son Erik Stone and his wife Erin. An opportunity to celebrate Michèle’s life and share memories together will be planned for late summer.
articles.title: Longtime arts champion Michèle Stone dies on May 15

articles.text: William T. (Bill) Ruth, passed away on March 15, 2021 in Piedmont, He was 82. Born in Newport, Rhode Island during a hurricane in 1938, Bill was the son of Col. Harold S. Ruth and Ruth T. Ruth. As an “army brat”, as he would call it, he was raised in the Philippines, and lived in Virginia, Boston, and in Tokyo from 1946-1950 during the occupation. His parents moved to Piedmont in 1953 and he graduated from Piedmont High School in 1956. He went on to UC Berkeley, where he was a part of the Phi Kappa Sigma fraternity. He was drafted into the military and served in Vietnam as the skipper of a Swift Boat. After returning to California, he graduated from UC Berkeley with a Master’s degree in Business Administration. He became a successful financial consultant for more than 30 years, including many development projects in San Francisco, Richmond and Stockton. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, June 2, 2021 Obituary Longtime arts champion Michèle Stone dies on May 15 Michèle Stone of Oakland, the life partner of Harry Howe, passed away peacefully in her sleep early in the morning of Saturday, May 15, 2021, at Kaiser Oakland Medical Center. She was 78. Born Michèle Dee Hyman in Santa Monica on July 14, 1942, she was the daughter of Frank and Yetta Hyman. Frank was an engineer and moved to various major jobs in Southern California, so she spent her early years in Los Angeles, Mojave, Twenty-nine Palms, Van Nuys, and Pomona before moving to a home in Claremont that her father had designed. After graduating from Claremont High School in 1960, she moved to the Bay Area, where she earned a Bachelor’s degree with a Decorative Arts major at UC Berkeley in 1964. She earned a lifetime teaching credential and first taught with Oakland Unified School District in 1966. She taught first- and second-grade classes in several different schools and managed to earn a Master’s in Education degree from Cal State Hayward. She taught at Crocker Highlands Elementary School for the last 34 years of a 42-year teaching career. The wonderful, full life that Michèle was able to build and enjoy in Oakland included a deep and constant commitment to the community and its future growth and well-being, as evidenced by her influence on the hundreds of children she taught with such dedication and satisfaction. Her membership for many years at Oakland’s Temple Sinai resulted in many lasting friendships spanning all walks of life, while providing her with emotional security and support whenever needed. She spent many years also as an active member of Women’s American ORT, helping The Piedmont Center for the Arts and other performing arts organizations lost one of the principal cheerleaders and supporters with the passing of Michèle Stone on May 15. to support a world-wide network of schools for both children and adults, and was instrumental in the establishment and operation of a local thrift store supporting both her temple and ORT. Michèle also had a deep love of the arts and performing arts and recognized the singular value they provide to communities. She was a collector of books and objects of visual and creative arts of all kinds. She was a supporter and subscriber of Oakland Symphony since the days when Calvin Simmons was its director, and was a moving force supporting the Symphony’s educational and outreach programs, donating hundreds of hours every season. She also was a strong supporter and constant volunteer with Piedmont Center for the Arts, where she typically was the first person in the front row for nearly all concerts. She and Harry were also longtime supporters of and regular attendees at concerts of the New Century Chamber Orchestra, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, the Philharmonia Baroque, Berkeley Symphony, and the SFJazz Center. Michèle loved the excitement of exploring new places and new ideas, traveling extensively and frequently throughout the United States, and throughout Western Europe and the Mediterranean and Aegean Sea areas. She always came home with new friends with whom she stayed in touch over the years. Wherever she went she would be greeted by young adults who had at one time been her students in their first years of elementary school, or adults whose children she had taught. When she was at home, she loved to explore new recipes, to cook for and entertain her many circles of friends, to work on and cherish her rose garden and extensive collection of orchids, and to play mah-jongg and socialize with those with whom she was closest. After all these years of giving, her final gift was to donate her remains to the UCSF Willed Body program, with the hope that she might thus contribute one day to a better outcome for another person, and at the same time relieving her surviving family members from the tasks involved with a funeral or burial. This final gift also relieves all who knew her from any obligation to travel to a specific location in order to visit her spirit, which will instead always be with all those she knew wherever you are. Gifts in memory of Michèle Stone may be made to Oakland Symphony, George Mark Children’s House, or Temple Sinai in Oakland. Michèle is survived by her life partner Harry Howe, her younger brother Steven Hyman, her son Adam, his wife Eran and daughter Emma, and her son Erik Stone and his wife Erin. An opportunity to celebrate Michèle’s life and share memories together will be planned for late summer. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Monday Book Group will have a book conversation this coming Monday, June 7, at 1:30 p.m. with Piedmont author Shanti Brien regarding her recently published book, Almost Innocent. Shanti is a practicing defense attorney and wife of a former NFL player. In her book she writes about our criminal justice system seen through her life experience and the stories of nine of her previously convicted felon clients. The conversation will be about a half hour before the reading group discusses its previously planned June selection. Those interested in learning more about Shanti and Almost Innocent can go to https://www.shantibrien. com/. Those interested in joining the First Monday Reading Group may contact John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department (jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov).

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

articles.text: Mountain View Cemetery recently reopened to the general public two days a week for limited recreational activities. The historic 226-acre cemetery has a long history of welcoming the public to enjoy its park-like space. It has been closed for more than a year due to the Covid pandemic. People may now visit on Saturdays and Wednesdays between 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Enter at the Piedmont Avenue gate. Center for Disease Control guidelines are in place and masks are required. All visitors are asked to be respectful of plots. Founded in 1863 and designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the architect of Central Park in New York City, Mountain View Cemetery is a private, non-profit cemetery providing mortuary services to the public; unlike other open spaces in Oakland, it does not receive any public funding. Costs to host the public are borne by plot owners. Dogs must be on leash and are not allowed on plots. No alcohol, loud vehicles and music, skateboards, or scooters are allowed in the cemetery. For more information, call 658-2588 Millionaires Row in historic Mountain View Cemetery at the end of Piedmont Avenue in Oakland

articles.text: Safeway opened a new store in Piedmont on Highland Avenue in 1940. The store has a mission tile roof, large plate glass windows in front and a faux chimney with a weathervane. The weathervane is faintly visible in the sign. To blend in with Piedmont’s residential nature, the store was designed in a Spanish Colonial style with a mission tile roof and a faux chimney with a weathervane. Like many Safeway stores designed at the time, the building had decorative pilasters (columns) on the parking lot side of the building. Fentons Creamery on Piedmont Avenue is a former Safeway and still has pilasters on the parking lot side. When the Highland Avenue store opened, Safeway sold prime rib roasts for 23 cents per pound, ground coffee for 18 cents for a 1-pound can, and Wheaties for 10 cents a box. The store thrived until 1970 when the company closed it as being too small. Safeway was building large, bright, modern supermarkets with large Another rare photo shows Safeway and the Flying A gas station on Highland Avenue. parking lots, and the store was too small to be remodeled. It lacked the space to carry the expanded line of groceries. The large plate glass windows in front, seen in the 1940 sketch and photo, have been filled in and replaced with an arched entry on Highland for the bank. Grand Avenue businesses Residents living near Grand Avenue had a series of grocery stores dating back to at least 1914. The former A Mon Chateau saloon at the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues became the Grand Avenue Grocery Company. By 1922, it was the Del Monte Market. In the 1930s, George and Jacob Leisz ran the grocery store. Piggly Wiggly, a division of Safeway, opened a second grocery store on the block at the corner of Sunnyside and Grand Avenues in the 1930s. In 1936, the old A Mon Chateau building was torn down, and a series of gas stations occupied the The Grand Avenue Grocery opened in 1914 in the former A Mon Chateau saloon. Grocery stores operated at this corner of Grand and Linda Avenues until 1935.
articles.title: The History of Piedmont

articles.text: Before we leave the history of central Piedmont, I would be remiss if I did not mention Piedmont’s Safeway store and other services. Hamby’s Market was the only grocery store in central Piedmont from 1915 to 1940. In addition to Hamby’s, Springman’s Pharmacy, and the Sweet Shop in the commercial center, Standard Oil operated a gas and service station by 1930. The expansion of Piedmont’s commercial center came after a long struggle. In 1929, the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance to allow businesses on Grand Avenue, on the west side from the city line to Linda Avenue, and on the east side from the city line to Fairview. Seven months later, voters turned down another zoning ordinance to extend the business district to Oakland Avenue. Today, the business district in Piedmont on Grand Avenue remains the same as it was in 1929. See more about the stores on Grand Avenue later in this article. More Stores For many years, the Piedmont City Council did “everything in its power to prevent the enlargement of the business district here,” according to news archives. Following a California Supreme Court decision in 1938, the Council reluctantly agreed to permit additional commercial development at Highland and Vista Avenues. In 1939, the Tidewater Oil Company built a gas station at the corner of Highland and Vista Avenues where Bank of America is currently located. It operated as the Flying A station into the late 1960s, when it became a Phillips 66 station. In 1940, Safeway Stores opened a new, modern supermarket at 333 Highland Avenue, occupying the space where both CitiBank and Mulberry’s Market are located. Officials at Safeway wanted to meet the wishes of the residents on the architecture and invited Piedmonters to an open meeting at City Hall to review and comment on the plans for the architecture of the new store. This rare photo shows the Chevron station and Highland Way, originally the Key System streetcar right of way. The narrow alley served Hamby’s Market for deliveries. Like many Safeway stores designed at the time, the building had decorative pilasters (columns) on the parking lot side of the building. Fentons Creamery This rare photo shows the Chevron station and Highland Way, originally the Key System streetcar right of way. The narrow alley served Hamby’s Market for deliveries. The Piedmont Historical Society invites you to become a member on Piedmont Avenue is a former Safeway and still has pilasters on the parking lot side. When the Highland Avenue store opened, Safeway sold prime rib roasts for 23 cents per pound, ground coffee for 18 cents for a 1-pound can, and Wheaties for 10 cents a box. The store thrived until 1970 when the company closed it as being too small. Safeway was building large, bright, modern supermarkets with large Another rare photo shows Safeway and the Flying A gas station on Highland Avenue. parking lots, and the store was too small to be remodeled. It lacked the space to carry the expanded line of groceries. The large plate glass windows in front, seen in the 1940 sketch and photo, have been filled in and replaced with an arched entry on Highland for the bank. Grand Avenue businesses Residents living near Grand Avenue had a series of grocery stores dating back to at least 1914. The former A Mon Chateau saloon at the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues became the Grand Avenue Grocery Company. By 1922, it was the Del Monte Market. In the 1930s, George and Jacob Leisz ran the grocery store. Piggly Wiggly, a division of Safeway, opened a second grocery store on the block at the corner of Sunnyside and Grand Avenues in the 1930s. In 1936, the old A Mon Chateau building was torn down, and a series of gas stations occupied the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues: Richfield Oil, Phillips Gas, and Leo Kraft’s Chevron. In the 1950s and 1960s, the Robert Foudy family operated Foudy’s Fine Foods at the corner of Grand and Sunnyside. It was a favorite spot for school children to buy candy after school. The store closed in 1967 when the family retired from the grocery business. Today, the Piedmont Financial Center occupies this block. articles.text: Less than 2 weeks until statewide reopening on June 15 Even as most Bay Area counties are now in the least restrictive tier for reopening their economy, the number of daily COVID- 19 cases in Alameda County remains too high for the county to move up tiers. However, in less than two weeks, most COVID-19 restrictions across the state will be eliminated. Until June 15, counties are still subject to the state’s color-coded four-tier reopening system. Yesterday, Tuesday, June 1, Marin and Monterey counties joined Santa Clara, Santa Cruz, San Francisco and San Mateo counties in the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier. Alameda County, along with Contra Costa, Napa, Solano and Sonoma counties, is in the second-least restrictive orange tier, or moderate tier. Alameda County has been in the orange tier since March 30. While most businesses can reopen with modifications in the orange tier, capacity limits and other restrictions are further reduced in the yellow tier. COVID-19 positivity in Alameda County is at 0.7 percent, its lowest level since the coronavirus pandemic began 14 months ago, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data on May 31. To move into the yellow tier, the positivity rate in Alameda County needs to stay below 2 percent. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to remain below 2.2 percent – it is currently 1.4 percent in Alameda County. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1, but right now there are 1.6 cases per 100,000, although this represents a decrease from last week. The new reopening guidelines that go into effect everywhere in California on June 15 abolish all COVID-19 capacity restrictions and physical distancing rules. For large outdoor events with over 10,000 participants, the state recommends that venues ask attendees for vaccination proof or a negative COVID-19 test. For large indoor events with over 5,000 participants, venues must require attendees to provide proof of vaccination or a negative test. Along with the wide reopening of the state’s economy, mask mandates will be mostly eliminated for fully vaccinated people on June 15. The new mask rules follow guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention released last month, which said fully vaccinated people can go without masks and social distancing in most situations. The CDC said that masks are only required for the vaccinated in certain instances, like on airplanes or buses. Instead of an immediate mandate change, California opted to wait several weeks to adopt the CDC guidance, a move applauded by Alameda County health officials. Masking guidelines are ultimately up to local and state governments, the CDC said. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 88,955, an increase of roughly 290 in the past seven days. There have been 27,741 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,750 cases in Hayward. Tragically, the total number of COVID-19 fatalities countywide is now 1,693. One new case of COVID-19 was reported in Piedmont across the past seven days. The total number of Piedmont cases since the pandemic began is 185. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,685,455 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 62,021 deaths due to the disease statewide. The state positivity rate is 0.7 percent, the same rate as Alameda County and a record low for California. read.” —Mary Salazar, The Country Bookshop, Southern Pines, NC A Ghost in the Throat lioasis, Memoir “This is a literary mystery explored with white-hot intensity. articles.text: State announces vaccine lottery California announced on Monday, May 31 that it had reached a goal set by President Joe Biden to inoculate 70 percent of the adult population with at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine by July 4. Alameda County surpassed the goal by reaching the 70 percent benchmark on May 10. California became the 11th state to reach the goal of 70 percent of the population with at least one dose. The state joined Pennsylvania, Vermont, Hawaii, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Maine, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and New Mexico. Soon after the declaration from Gov. Gavin Newsom, Maryland announced that it had become the 12th state to reach Biden’s goal. California has the biggest population of any of the 12 states by a large margin. The White House set its vaccination goal for the nation on May 4. Three vaccines are available in the United States. Pfizer and Moderna vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. A vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson requires only one dose. To incentivize Californians toward total vaccination, Newsom last week unveiled the “Vax for the Win” program that will award millions of dollars to vaccinated Californians in a lottery. Any California resident, including those under the age of 18, who has received at least one dose will be eligible to win $50,000 or $1.5 million. This Friday, June 4, 15 people will win $50,000. Another 15 will win $50,000 on June 11 and 10 people will be awarded $1.5 million on June 15. The next 2 million Californians to get fully vaccinated will receive a $50 gift card. “California has already made incredible progress in the fight against COVID-19, with the lowest case rates in the country while administering millions more vaccines than any other state,” Newsom said in a statement last week. “But we aren’t stopping there, we’re doing everything it takes to get Californians vaccinated as we approach June 15 to help us fully reopen safely.” As of Sunday, May 30, 1.83 million doses of vaccine have been administered in Alameda County. Almost 76 percent of the county’s population ages 12 and older, over 1 million people, are partially vaccinated. Almost 60 percent of eligible people in the county, about 847,000 people, are fully vaccinated. Piedmont continues to be the most vaccinated municipality in the county. Nearly 97 percent of residents ages 12 and older, an estimated 8,983 people, have received at least one dose of vaccine. Almost 74 percent of City residents ages 12 and older, some 6,862 people, have been fully vaccinated. In Oakland, 74 percent of the eligible population is partially vaccinated, and 57 percent is fully vaccinated. Pfizer received emergency approval for children ages 12 to 15 on May 13. Since then, over 33,300 kids in this age group have received their first dose of vaccine. This amounts to over 40 percent of this demographic in the county. Both Pfizer and Moderna are currently conducting vaccine trials in children as young as 6 months old. Dr. Anthony Fauci, the Chief Medical Advisor to the White House, has said that he expects all children will be eligible for vaccination by the end of the year. All three vaccine manufacturers have received emergency use authorization to produce vaccines, but Moderna yesterday, Tuesday, June 1, began applying for a full license from the Food and Drug Administration. Pfizer applied for full approval for their vaccine for people ages 16 and older in early May. Additionally, health officers for all Bay Area counties announced on Friday, May 28 that children and adults can receive other vaccinations along with their COVID-19 vaccine. “We know a lot of people have delayed getting care and regular immunizations during the pandemic,” Dr. Chris Farnitano, health officer for Contra Costa County, said in a statement. “This new guidance will make it easier for people to catch up on any immunizations they’re due for when they get a COVID- 19 vaccine at their provider’s office.” COVID-19 vaccines are available for free to all Alameda County residents ages 12 and older. Appointments are not required at many vaccination locations in Oakland and elsewhere in the county. As of press time, same-day appointments were available at several locations in Oakland and Berkeley. Alameda County links to available vaccine appointments at covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines

articles.text: Pursuant to Section 4.04(A) of the Piedmont City Charter, residents are hereby notified that at 6:00 p.m. on June 7, 2021 the Piedmont City Council will hold a public hearing regarding the proposed City budget and fee schedule for fiscal year 2021-2022. The Council will hold an additional meeting at 6:00 p.m. on June 21, 2021. Consistent with Executive Orders No. N-25-20 and No. N-29- 20 from the Executive Department of the State of California and the Alameda County Health Official’s Shelter in Place Orders, the City Council meeting will not be physically open to the public and City Council members will be teleconferencing into each meeting via Zoom Teleconference. The specific teleconference details will be available on the agenda for each meeting. At the same meetings, the City Council will hold public hearings regarding the Municipal Services Tax and Municipal Sewer Tax and will set the tax rates for the fiscal year 2021-2022. Copies of the proposed budget are available for public inspection on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. A limited number of paper copies of the budget are available from the City Clerk’s office. You can email cityclerk@piedmont.ca.gov or telephone (510) 420-3040, between the hours of 8:30 a.m. and 12:00 noon, and 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. to request a copy. John O. Arriving in Mexico one day ahead of 320 volunteers from Piedmont Community Church, Tom Huffaker (left), Garrett Kail, Mike Bandrowski, Ron Heckmann, Rod Brown, Wayne Marzolf, and Pav Wilkinson helped prepare the work site where 20 houses will be built this week – the church’s annual teen mission trip during Spring Break. To show they were homesick, they gathered to take a peek at the Post on Saturday, April 13. Previously published in the Piedmont Post on April 17, 2019. Send your photos of the Post in the far corners of the world, or of other communities named Piedmont, to: WITWAW, 1139 Oakland Ave., Piedmont, 94611.
